Mr. Speaker, I rejoiced, in common, I presume with most citizens of Canada, when I heard the speech of the Finance Minister setting forth the financial affairs of this country. The satisfaction I experienced was doubtless felt by all on this side of the House as

well as by our friends on the other side, though perhaps their satisfaction was dampened a little by the fact that such magnificent progress had taken place in our country during the term of a Liberal administration, and that it had never obtained while they had control of our affairs. It was also a matter of satisfaction to learn that the government had discharged their duties while they were lately in Great Britain in endeavouring to obtain a preference in the British market. That they were unsuccessful was not their fault. They evidently did all they could to obtain what our friends on	at present of no use to the people of the United States as a protection, they could increase their trade, by all means let them reduce the duty. But, Sir, a preference of that kind offered to us that will not interfere with any of the protected industries of the United States, would be of such limited value to us that it would be impossible for us to accept it. The idea that the United States will ever allow us reciprocity in natural products, for a right to sell their manufactured goods in Canada under the present tariff, is expecting entirely too much. I am therefore confident that there will be
but were unsuccessful. It Was also a matter of satisfaction for us on this side of the House to learn that the government did not fail to do their duty, when it was forced upon them by the action of the German government, by retaliating in adopting a surtax on German goods. There is a misconception as to how far this surtax will operate; but if it prevents, as 1 believe it will, the importation of German goods made in England,which has been going on for a long time past, it will go far to remove the difficulties under which some of the manufacturers of this country labour at the present time. As I understand it, if 51 per cent of the pidce of a finished product represents the German portion of the work, the article comes under the operation of the surtax, and is placed on the general list to which an addition of 33J per cent is added. Therefore, if that surtax is applied as it should be applied, it will prohibit from entering into this country the German goods that are made in England, and almost prohibit the importation into this country of goods that are made in Germany. Now, I am quite willing to admit that our hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) may feel hopeful of some reciprocity arrangements being entered into with the people of the United States. That, apparently, has been the one -object of his life. Personally, I am not so hopeful as he appears to be, because in my own mind I have not the slightest idea that anything will ever come of our attempt to have reciprocal arrangements with the people of the United States. From their public men, who have a right to speak with authority because they know the opinions of the people for whom they speak, we have never yet heard one utterance which would justify us in believing that they would concede to Canada any reciprocal arrangements that it would be in our interest to accept. President Roosevelt, for instance, has distinctly laid down the conditions upon which a foreign country can have reciprocity with the United States. This reciprocity must not interfere with their manufacturing, their industrial, and their commercial interests. The late Mr. McKinley also laid down the same doctrine in a clear and emphatic manner. He said that if by lowering the duties that are 56*	United States, believing that they will never offer reciprocity on such terms as it would be our interest to accept. Nor do I believe that what has recently taken place in the House of Commons of Great Britain gives us any reason to expect that we will get a preference in Great Britain for many years to come. We did hope that the imposition of the duty upon flour and wheat would give the British people an opportunity to grant us a preference without putting a tax on the British people, but I understand that that duty has been wiped out, so hostile was it to the feelings of our friends across the ocean. I see no prospect in the immediate future, either for a reciprocity treaty with the United States, or for a preferential treaty with Great Britain; and now that the grain duties have been removed, I see no reason why this government should not be able, when the necessity present itself to rearrange the tariff of this country in such a way as will be in the best interests of all classes of the people. It may be that under present circumstances courtesy demands us to wait, because Mr. Chamberlain has not had an opportunity of exerting his influence in favour of the preference. It may be judicious as well as courteous to our American friends also not to anticipate the deliberations of the commission that has been appointed, seeing that the first move towards reciprocity has emanated from our friends across the line. But after we shall have found that our hopes in obtaining reciprocity with the United States, or a preference in Great Britain, are in vain, one of the principal reasons will be removed which have made us unwilling to interfere with the preference that has existed in the past; and the government has promised us that they will exercise a free hand in that matter, and that they will abolish the preference if it is seen to be needed in the interests of Canada. I am also gratified to learn, from the papers that were brought down, that the efforts of the government to prevent the scheduling of Canadian cattle in the British market, were put forth with force, with skill, and with earnestness, and their failure to get that embargo removed was due, as I believe, and as all the members of this

House believe, to a desire on tlie part of the British people to protect the raising of animals in that country. With all these facts before us, we have a right to assume that we will be able in the near future to rearrange our own tariff, if it is necessary, entirely in the interests of our own people. I can assure the Minister of Finance and the government that their desire to build up in this country the industry of the manufacture of steel rails, and for that purpose to give a substantial bonus, meets with the enthusiastic support, not only of their supporters on this side of the House, but also of our friends on the other side.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have been treated to a few addresses on the budget speech, and on what I will call for courtesy's sake, the amendment that is before the House. I regret to say that the hon. gentlemen who have spoken so far have not even alluded to that amendment, although it is one of considerable importance; but they have criticised the financial administration of our affairs, which, as was clearly pointed out last night by Mr. Speaker, is contrary to the rules of the House, but which, by the courtesy of the Minister of Finance, we are to continue to-day.
Our hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) was the last speaker last night, and he was terribly exercised over the fact that we have had a surplus amounting to some $40,000,000 during the period of our administration. He asked :	What did we
do with it ? What would he expect a wise and judicious administration to do with a surplus of some $40,000,000, but to invest it prudently in the interest of the people of Canada ? He instanced as a parallel case the farmer, who, after seven years of plenty had not succeeded in paying off the mortgage on his house, and he asked what would be thought of such a person. He went on to say that this would be a very foolish farmer, but that would depend upon conditions. If the farmer had taken the surplus of his labour and invested it building new bams, in draining his ground and in improving the productive power of his farm, he would have done much more wisely than to have applied it towards paying off the mortgage, which, in the case of the Dominion of Canada, only costs about 3 per cent. The government were wise in not reducing the debt, but in judiciously expending that money. But, he goes on to ask :	How long can the people stand this
tremendous expenditure ? He predicted that the day of reckoning is soon to come. Let us look and see how the people have stood it during past years, and if the present conditions obtain, how long they are likely to stand it. The best evidence of that is to ascertain what effect this large expenditure and these large surpluses of ours have had upon the welfare of our people. I presume it would be fair to direct the attention of the hon. gentleman to Mr. HEYD.
the amount of deposits the people have in the large chartered banks of tills country. In 1890 they amounted to $128,000,000. Six years after the time they were not so profusely bled as they say we are bleeding people now, the deposits had increased to $183,000,000, or in six years, only $55,000,000 had been added, while, during the last six years, while they have been paying such a tremendous tribute to the country, the deposits of the people increased from $183,000,000 to $382,000,000, or an increase of $199,000,000. It strikes me that the people are standing it, and at the same time improving their ovjn condition very perceptibly. I am quite content, myself, to believe that they are quite willing to continue such a state of affairs. Hon. gentlemen opposite appear to think that a surplus is an insuperable obstacle to the country's progress. They must remember that they also have had surpluses in times past. In 1882 and in 1883 they had a surplus amounting to $14,000,000. We have to go a long time back in order to get a surplus of that kind. After seventeen years experience, we do not find any more, but in these two years they had a surplus of $14,000,000. But, compare the conditions of the country then with the conditions of the country to-day. While they had a surplus of $14,000,000, the savings of the people in the banks of the country diminished from $97,000,000 to $95,000,000, so that the people were $2,000,000 poorer during their period of surpluses, while they were $199,000,000 richer during our period of surpluses. I think the country need have no special anxiety about these surpluses of ours. I owe my hon. friend from East Grey a slight apology for last night stating that the duty upon meat was of no benefit to the farmers of this country. I understood him to say wheat, but he was talking about meat, and I am quite willing to confess that it was of great benefit to the people of this country.
Hear, hear.

There is another thing I would like to draw your attention to, Mr. Speaker, and it is the few remarks that were made by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), that were not replied to by my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis). The hon. member for Bothwell alluded to the period of deficits. He appeared to feel proud that there had been deficits amounting to $5,694,758 in the three years ending the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, and he made it a charge against us that we had $20,994,445 to our credit at the end of the last three years, and in order to get over that difficulty he condemned the system of bookkeeping. He said our system of bookkeeping was all wrong. Well, it is the system we have inherited from the old government, the system that has been carried down since the period of confederation, and though the hon.

gentleman lias been a member of this House he never before raised his voice to find fault with our system of keeping our books. But, I can readily understand why he should find fault with our system when it shows quite clearly that our surpluses amounted to $20,994,445 in the last three years, while lion, gentlemen opposite had three years of deficits. In order to get over the difficulty, he takes the expenditure, both consolidated and capital, and says : See, they had no surplus because they were behind at the end of their period of time and actually increased the net debt of the people of this country. Well, that is true, but I claim still that the present system of keeping our accounts is correct, that it has ' always been correct and it never has been objected to except by the hon. member for Bothwell and the late Minister of Finance, who also found fault with it when it continued to show surpluses as a result of the good management of the Liberal party. But, if this contention is true to-day, where would the Conservative party be a few years ago ? Their receipts in 1884 were $31,000,000, their expenditure $57,000,000, showing a deficit of $26,000,000. Where would they have been in 1885 with a deficit of $16,000,000, where would they have been in 1880 with a deficit of $28,000,000, or a deficit of $70,000,000 in three years, and with an increase in the national debt of the people of $64,691,000 ? No system of bookkeeping can get over that. We are obliged to keep our books that way, but if the hon. gentleman is right now, they must have been wrong then, and these expenditures must be explained. Hon. gentlemen opposite say they are easily explained. The old government were building the Canadian Pacific Railway, and it was necessary to exceed the income of the country. This has been the case and this is our excuse to-day, that notwithstanding that we have been in receipt of large revenues we have engaged in large capital expenditures. But, our hon. friend goes on to say that the national debt is the true balance of the account when the final summing up takes place. I say that too. I say it is quite immaterial whether you charge the expenditure to consolidated account or capital account except for certain purposes, and that in the end it all comes to the increase in the national debt. Let us look at that for a short period of time. Our friends opposite increased the national debt in the three years ending 1896 by $17,000,000. We increased the national debt in the three years ending 1902 by $5,556,000. If we take the debt as it stood in 1897 at $261,538,596, which was the time when we got absolute control of our affairs, and take the actual debt on the 31st March, 1903, which was $261,620,000, we find that it was only $82,000 more than it was when we got control of the affairs of this country. That is the position to-day in connection with the national debt. Our hon.
friend (Mr. Clancy) had a great deal of fault to find with the tariff duties, and he tried hard to convince the country that the people of Canada were not paying the duty, and that the raising of the tariff would not increase the burdens on the people. If that be true, then all our efforts to remove the preference are absolutely of no use. But we have been told time and again, and we know it is true, that the preference in favour of Great Britain has reduced the price of goods in Canada, has brought disaster upon the woollen mills, and that the manufacturers want the preference removed and the full duty restored. Do they want that in order to still further increase their tariff r no, they want it to stiffen prices and to remove the tremendous competition that they are subject to because of this preference. It is of no use at this late date to try to make people believe that by increasing the tariff you do not increase the price of goods.
Hear, hear.

The gentlemen who spoke on the other side have kept a long way off from the amendment that is before the House. I desire Sir, to confine my attention particularly to that amendment and to see just what it means. But let me say Sir, that the hon. gentleman from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) owes an apology to the leader of the House as well to the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) for the statement he made last night to the effect that Mr. Charlton was inspired by the Prime Minister to make his speech and that the sentiments entertained by Mr. Charlton are those entertained by the leader of the government. The member for Bothwell told us that he got this information from Mr. Charlton himself. I deny that. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) was told by the member for North Norfolk that he would speak at a certain time at the request of the premier, but to hold the premier responsible for the utterances of Mr. Charlton and then to say that Mr. Charlton himself was the author of the story, is something that we on this side will not believe.
I thought it was the devil and not the Prime Minister that inspired the speech of Mr. Charlton.

Well, you will admit at all events that the Prime Minister is not the devil. Now the amendment which has been presented to the House is couched in very ambiguous terms as are all the statements with reference to the tariff which are formulated by gentlemen on the other side. I have taken considerable trouble to ascertain what the meaning of the word ' adequate ' is. I find in the dictionaries that the words ' sufficient ' or ' enough ' are very fair equivalents, but when you begin to apply words to a thing of vast importance like the tariff of Canada, it is well to be definite. In

order to find out just what the Conservative party means by the word 'adequate' we have to go to a little town in Manitoba to illustrate it in a practical way. The leader of the opposition and his friends were in Manitoba last summer and a poet in that country hearing what they said, although he might have applied himself with much better advantage to something else, got off this version of adequate protection.
Through a western town called Morden Passed a famous man called Borden Who, in a tone articulate The problem tried to demonstrate That duties, that were adequate Would be a boon, as sure as fate.
To the merry men of Morden If they'd only bear the burden.
But the men in Western Morden With contempt refused the burden. Though he did his best to stimulate,
They thought he did but simulate.
So they more and more do hesitate To believe that duties adequate Would relieve the men of Morden Of the heavy useless burden.
That is an interpretation of the word ' adequate ' as used by the leader of tlie opposition. We all know that Mr. Hugh John Macdonald had promised the people of Manitoba that if the Conservative party were returned to power they would have free agricultural implements and while the leader of the opposition was delivering his speech in the town of Morden some one asked :	What about free agricultural implements. The Winnipeg ' Telegram ' which I presume gives a fair report has the following account of what happened. The leader of the opposition replied as follows to the question
Question : What about free agricultural implements promised by Mr. Macdonald ?

I will answer my friend's question before I sit down so definitely that there will be no question about it. I will answer on behalf of the Liberal-Conservative party which has no Sifton at one end and Tarte at the other.
Question : Will you raise the duty ?

We will make the duty adequate and if it is now high enough, * as I believe it is,' to enable manufacturers to make implements in Canada, we will not increase it. I am informed that implements are as cheap in Canada as in the United States. So the duty seems high enough.
The leader of the opposition tells us that ' adequate ' means to enable manufacturers to make goods in Canada. It is to that interpretation of the word that I shall address my remarks. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) tells us that ' adequate ' means to enable manufacturers of cotton or wool or steam engines or anything else to make them in Canada if the duty is high enough to secure that, and that there is no Tarte at one end and no Sifton at the other end to preach a high tariff or a low tariff as the case may be. He told us that the word Mr. HEYD.
' adequate ' meant a duty high enough to enable manufacturers to make implements in Canada, and that he believed the duty on agricultural implements is high enough.
Do the Conservatives intend that the plough makers and the binder makers and the agricultural implement makers of Canada should believe that ' adequate ' means the ability to manufacture in this country. Is it for that that the manufacturers' associations are giving banquets and inducing the Hon. Mr. Tarte to make speeches. Do they not mean something else by the word ' adequate.' That word ' adequate ' is the crux of the whole question.
If the leader of the opposition is right that the word ' adequate ' means a tariff that would enable the manufacturer to make goods in Canada reserving to himself a reasonable and a fair profit; then we are all adequate protectionists. I do not think you will find on this side of the House even the most pronounced free trader who would object to that kind of adequate protection. But concealed behind that word ' adequate ' is something that we do not understand. The manufacturer believes it means high tariff, so high as to secure Canada for the Canadian manufacturers. That is what we think is meant by that word ' adequate,' and with that catch phrase, hon. gentlemen opposite will not raise the duty on agricultural implements; they say that is high enough. They go from one end of the country to the other, and, with such an amendment as is presented to this House, vague and meaningless, they fool the people, as they attempted to fool the people away up in that western town of Morden.
Now, let us see what that resolution means in its practical application. It reads as follows :
This House regarding the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at al'l times secure the Canadian market for Canadians ;
The hon. gentleman's first proposition is to protect labour. Well, I want somebody who has more ability than I have to devise some plan whereby labour can be protected. Labour is as free as air, and gravitates to the points where wages are most remunerative. It leaves the points where wages become less than is necessary for the maintenance of the labourers ; it is constantly shifting ; and it cannot be protected or, if it can be, then, what I hold in my hand is absolutely meaningless. I have here the proceedings of the Trades and Labour Council of the Dominion of Canada at their annual meeting held in the city of Berlin and attended by the representatives of one hundred and two organizations. Are these men entitled to speak for labour, or is our friend who leads the opposition ? That meeting passed the following resolution :

Whereas the Manufacturers' Association has declared its intention to seek an increase in the tariff, and, whereas, the injury and oppression of industry comes not from the various industries offering to exchange riches for riches, but from the extortions to which labour is subjected by the holders of the land, the forests, the mines and oljjer natural opportunities, therefore this congress would condemn any increase in the tariff, and would urge that taxes be removed as soon as possible to those values which now enable non-production to impoverish industry.
That is the opinion of one hundred and two labour organizations, met for the purpose of considering how they could advance their own interests. That resolution passed unanimously, and I say that these representative labour men in convention assembled are more entitled to say what will conduce to the interests of labour than even the hou. leader of the opposition, and this whole House along with him. I, therefore, say that the hon. gentleman's resolution, in its application to the first part of the population whom it proposes to protect, is absolutely ineffective, but, on the contrary, is injurious.
Now, let us see to what other classes it applies. In our trade returns we divide the interests of Canada into about six classes :	Mining, fishing, forests, animals, agriculture and manufactures. Let us take the miners first. The exports of our mines last year amounted to $34,947,575. The resolution proposes by adequate protection to benefit them. How can the miners out in the Yukon, who have everything to buy, and who have to take their returns out of the soil, be protected by increasing the prices of their tools and their food, while in no way providing them with a market V They are a class who cannot be protected no matter how much we try. It is true, the lead miners in British Columbia are just now subjected to a terrible inconvenience ; but this is not particularly for the want of protection. It is because an organized trust in the United States will not buy their ore. If they could secure a market for their ore, they would not ask for protection ; but they are asking for protection for lead ore, because they have no foreign market for it; and so far as I am personally concerned, I will endorse the action of the Minister of Finance if he will put such a duty on everything into which lead enters as will enable these men to live, in the particular circumstances in which they are placed. At the same time, do not let us try to persuade ourselves that we can, by a policy of adequate protection, advance the interests of the miners of this country.
Can we do it with our fisheries ? They exported last year $14,143,294 worth of fish, besides supplying nearly the entire requirements of the country, and they were subjected to a competition of how much ? Six hundred and twenty thousand seven hundred and six dollars, consisting of :	Oysters, $240,000 ; fish bait, $101,088 ; anchovies and sardines, $107,000 ; and forty-three other items, amounting to $172,018. Therefore, it is impossible for adequate protection to advance the interests of our great fishing industries.
Let us now turn to the lumbering industry, which is sufficiently large to warrant us in devoting a little time to its consideration. Our exports of forest products last year, amounted to $32,119,420, and our imports to $4,242,358, including $941,000 of oak and $065,000 of logs and round timber. Add the imports of fancy woods, such as we have not got in this country, amounting to $1,000,000 or $1,500,000, and the lumber required for the people of the North-west who are many miles from a lumber yard, and you have all the foreign lumber brought into Canada. Have we had any delegations from the labour interests, the mining industry, except the lead miners, the fishing industry or the lumber interest, asking us by means of a protective tariff to better their conditions ? Not at all.
The greatest industry which we have in this country is that of animals and animal products. That has taken on a wonderful development during the last few years. Our exports of animals and their products last year amounted to $59,161,209. Let us look at this question in an honest, candid way, and ask ourselves if we can improve tbe condition of the farmers by giving them adequate protection. The leader of the opposition tried the other day to show that they are subjected to a tremendous competition. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce showed that out of the $28,000,000 of agricultural products that were imported, not more than $6,000,000 came into competition with the products of our farmers. Of the actual imports of last ye*r which our cattle-growers had to face, amounting to $3,000,000, there were $1,064,988 of animals, $1,716,747 of food products and $375,515 of stock for breeding purposes, while we exported $59,000,000 worth of our surplus product, after supplying the requirements of our own people. How can you protect that great industry by increasing the protection of the farmers. They have no competition now. You might raise the duty to 100 per cent, and it would be of no benefit to the farmers, except that in an indirect sense it would produce a home market for some of their surplus products.
Take our agricultural returns, take last year we exported $37,000,000 of our surplus products and our exports of these products are likely to increase in much greater ratio than they have done in the past. But what competition were our agriculturists subjected to ? We must not forget that it is not the amount we import into this country which comes into competition with our own products, but the amount consumed in this country. It is the quantity imported for

home consumption which competes with our own products, and the hon. leader of the opposition seeks to create a false impression when he says we imported some $7,000,000 or $S,000,000 worth of wheat last year. What we imported from the west went out of this country by the east. It merely passed through this country, yet the hon. gentleman would have us believe that that importation of wheat came into competition with what was raised by our own farmers. Out of $489,000 worth of grain which came into this country, the actual amount that did enter into competition with our own products was $89,000 worth. If we included corn, which we imported at the request and for the benefit of our farmers, the whole amount of agricultural products that came into competition with the products of our own farmers was but $5,700,000. When we consider these facts, must we not conclude that the resolution of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition goes a good deal further than the circumstances justify, when it calls on us to declare that our agricultural industry requires to be stimulated by an adequate tariff. It seems to me perfectly clear that, with the exception of a few manufacturing industries, there is no industry in this country that could be stimulated by an increased tariff, and during the past six years the output of our manufacturing industries has increased from $9,365,000 in 1896 to $18,462,000 last year. Even with regard to our manufacturing industries, the word adequate production has no significance, because, with the exception of a few, they are in a fairly prosperous condition, and when such a condition obtains they evidently enjoy what the hon. leader of the opposition calls an adequate protective tariff.
*The hon. gentleman read an extract from an interview with certain miners, in which the miners contended that the duty on wheat of twelve cents, on oats of ten cents, on hay of $2 a ton, and on eggs, three cents a dozen, bore very heavily upon them. The hon. gentleman was not suggesting that the protection given the farmers was too high. On the contrary, he thought it was not high enough. He believed that on certain agricultural products the duty should be increased so that a country like Canada, possessing agricultural capabilities second to none in the w'orld, should not be obliged to import from the United States nearly $28,000,000 of agricultural products and produce of animals. But, if he had said that out of this $28,000,000 of imports from the United States, $22,000,000 consisted of bananas and oranges and other articles in which our farmers are not interested, he would have presented a truthful statement. In declaring, however, that our imports of agricultural products amounted to $28,000,000 and then proceeding to base the argument he did on that statement, he produced a false impression. In order to obtain an Mr. HEYD.
accurate idea of the facts, I have looked into the Trade and Navigation Returns and I find that our imports were as follows :
Animals	$1,064,000
Grain	 489,000
And so on down, giving them the benefit of free corn and every conceivable thing that could possibly come into competition with the products of our Canadian farmers. The total importation amounts as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, to about $6,290,000. How does this compare with the total products of the Canadian farm ? It is estimated by the Bureau of Industries of Ontario that our agricultural products last year amounted to $214,000,000. It was estimated years ago by the Dominion statistician that the agricultural products of (lie Dominion amounted to over $500,000,000. I believe he was over the mark but now we have probably reached that stage. I put the question. If we raise $500,000,000 worth of agricultural products, how can an importation of only $5,000,000 worth affect our market-an importation of only about one per cent of our whole product ? To say that such a small percentage of imports could affect the prices of our gross production seems to me a patent absurdity.
Let me see how this thing works out when we apply the figures. The hon. gentleman says that we allowed wheat in subject to a duty of 12 cents per bushel, well, last year we imported $89,000 worth and this country raised $100,000,000 worth. How much benefit would accrue to the farmers by increasing the duty on wheat ? On oats the duty is 10 cents per bushel and the hon. gentleman wants that duty raised. But, I find that the total quantity of oats we imported was but $71,000 worth and that the province of Ontario alone raised $28,000,000 worth. What proportion does our importation of oats bear to the quantity we raise ? It is almost infinitesimal and microscopic. We might almost call it a specimen of bacteria which we are called on to consider in connection with this question. On hay, the duty is $2 per ton, and we imported $121,000 worth, the bulk of which I presume went into British Columbia or some of those distant territories which our Ontario farmers cannot reach. Our production of hay in Ontario alone last year amounted to $37,000,000, and we are asked to believe that this importation of $121,000 worth of hay comes into competition with the entire production of hay of this Dominion, and that to keep it out of this country would be a great service to our agriculturists. Then take potatoes, we imported last year $102,000 worth. But Ontario alone raised $7,000,000 worth, and included in that importation of $102,000 worth are sweet potatoes and yams. Are we to believe that by raising the duty from 15 to 45 cents a bushel, our people would be enabled to raise

sweet potatoes and yams, and that we would thereby introduce a new industry into Canada ? My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, even spoke of the advantage which increased protection would give our milk and cheese. Well, we imported milk to the extent of $55,000 worth, and cheese to the extent of $42,000 worth, and we are asked seriously to believe that this importation is a danger and a menace to the dairy industries of this country, which last year fed our own population of five and a half millions, and exported $19,000,000 worth of cheese and $6,000,000 worth of butter.
1 do not see anything in that resolution which throws out much encouragement to any of our industries. But I agree with the hon. the leader of the opposition on the importance of the home market to the people of Canada. I am of the opinion that that is a market which may be cultivated and developed, and which the government can cultivate and develop by-I will not call it a protective tariff for that term might be offensive to some of my friends-but by a tariffs for revenue. I believe that a tariff of revenue to a greater extent would be useful to the people of this country, and I shall try briefly to show by the trend of our trade during the past few years, that an absolute necessity for successful farming in Canada is the establishment of a home market. If we take the two great branches of the farming industry-agricultural products and animals-we will find that we have got two countries in the world to sell to and almost three to buy from. Of our entire exports, no less than 90 per cent goes to Great Britain and the United States; and of our entire imports we get 85 per cent from Great Britain and the United States. Germany supplies, of our imports, something over $10,000,000 and takes of our exports about $1,300,000. So, we cannot get hurt very much if they put a prohibitive tariff on our goods. We can eliminate the world in considering what the future lias in store for us. With only 15 per cent of our imports coming from countries other than Great Britain and the United States, and only 10 per cent of our exports going to the other countries, the proportion is so small as to have practically no effect. After seven years, we find that we have increased our exports to Great Britain by over $38,000,000, while our exports to the United States have increased only a little over $1,000,000. Now, let us look the facts in the case from the farmers standpoint, and consider, in view of the limited market in the world at large and in the United-States, what chance we have in the British market and in the market we can create for our own products among our own people. That is the proposition the farmers have to meet. It is no use for them to say to themselves :	We want to sell in the
dearest market and buy in the cheapest market. That would be an ideal condition, and may come when the millennium comes; but it is not here just now. The nations of the world simply say ; We. will not buy from you. That is what the United States tell us. It tells our farmers, with their surplus of $100,000,000 : We will only take five or six millions of certain qualities of your goods and the rest you can do what you like with. The question naturally arises, a question of considerable importance -is the market of Great Britain an unlimited market; can we continue for all time to send our export products to Great Britain ? Is there a time likely to come in the near future when we shall reach the limit of the demand for consumption in that country ? With the United States markets closed against us, with Germany, France and all the nations of the world with highly protective tariffs, our outlook as farmers is simply the outlook upon the British market and the home market-and the local market is of even more importance than the British market. Now you will bear in mind that Canada, at the present time is an agricultural country. The proportion of farmers to the rest of the community is as three to two. It has been changing, and changing rapidly, during the past ten years. Owing to the influx that has taken place of people going to our North-west, the present condition of affairs may continue and we may remain; an agriculltutral (community. But it is changing in the United States. That has ceased to be an agricultural country and has become a manufacturing country,

for the proportion of farmers to others there is ten to twenty-one. Now, we are in the peculiar position still of being an agricultural country, capable for years to come of supplying far in excess of our wants, with the markets of the world, except Great Britain, barred against us. Therefore I say the development of a home market is a matter of great importance to the people of Canada. And the only way it can be done is by the application of a tariff for revenue purposes. The productive power of our farms last year was $500,000,000. We exported $100,000,000 worth, leaving $400,000,000 worth at home, of which, I presume, the rural population consumed at least one-half. It must not be forgotten that during the past year the rural population in old Canada has decreased by 112,000, while the urban population has increased by 364,000. In the province of Ontario, the farmers have decreased by 48,000, while the inhabitants of the cities, towns and villages have increased by 110,000. How much of our prosperity must be attributed to this change of population it is hard to say. It is commonly said that our prosperity is due to our export of farm products. But then, we consume in old Canada twice as much as we export. There are two or three ways open to us to enlarge the home market. Hon. gentlemen on the other side would say :	If you
have a highly protective tariff, that will cause all the goods required in this country to be manufactured in the country, and so yon will increase the urban population to such an extent that the farmers will have a population for their surplus products. Is that likely to be the case ? The United States tariff of 50 per cent! meets us when we seek to enter their market. In relation to grain, there is an unlimited market for many years in Great Britain. The imports of grain and flour into Britian last year, was $150,000,000. We have a long time to develop even the North-west before we can overtake that market, so that my present remarks do not apply to Manitoba and the North-west. But the old Dominion of Canada has ceased to be an exporter of grain. We hardly raise more than we ourselves consume. So, we are compelled to build up a different system of production in order to have an export trade. We have developed in a wonderful degree during the past few years the cheese industry, the bacon industry and the cattle industry. These are the three largest. Are we likely to overtake the consuming capacity of the British market in these lines ? Of cheese last year we exported to Great Britain $20,0001000 worth. The lentjire import in|to Great Britain in that year was $31,000,000. We have reached 65 per cent of the cheese trade of the British market, and it is the opinion now of men engaged in this business that we are exporting as much cheese as we are likely to do, unless, by improving Mr. HEYD.
the quality of the cheese, we may improve the desire to consume our cheese by the English people, in which ease that increase wrill be held by the Canadian makers of cheese. Take bacon, the next in importance of our exports last year, amounting to $12,400,000, whereas the consuming capacity of hog products in Great Britain was represented by an importation of $68,000,000 last year. There appears to be a big margin between $12,000,000 and $68,000,000, and people assume that all we have to do.is to go in and capture that market. But that is a delusion. Mr. Flavelle, the head of the Davies Pork Packing Company, in an address that he recently made before the Pig Breeders' Association of Canada, says that that is an entirely erroneous impression ; that we have already reached the extent of our bacon producing capacity ; that while the English people import some $68,000,000 worth of hog products, a large proportion of that is of the heavy, coarse hogs in which we cannot compete with the people of the United States, who can sell that class of hogs cheaper than we can ; so in that market the United States is supreme. With Denmark, England and Ireland as competitors, we may hold our own, will hold our own, and may capture any further increase that may be developed for Wiltshire bacon. In cattle we exported $9,000,000 worth out of a possible $44,000,000 worth. I am not a cattle man, I do not know what prospects there are for further developing that trade. We have competitors in the United States who can produce cattle as good as we can, and a little cheaper, because their corn is cheaper. We have competitors in Argentina and other places, where food is cheap and labour is cheap, and I have grave doubts whether we can materially increase even our exports of cattle. Therefore, the question presents itself with force to the farming community. Are these things true, and if true, wherein is the remedy ?

Where can I get that Information ? Mr. HEYD. Any farmer in the House can tell you. I am not a farmer. Mr. GOURLEY. I can understand that they would have some advantage over us. Mr. HEYD. There are two or three theories, but I do not know. Now what .alternatives have our farmers got ? First, they have the important one of developing the home market. Every additional consumer in Canada is a benefit to the farming community. If, by a rearrangement of our tariff, our industries were injured so that the urban population that is now the principal consumers for our farmers were compelled to leave this country, at once the farming industry would be depressed. But if, by a judicious and wise system of tariff reduction, this urban population can be increased, the manufactured goods that we get abroad in many lines would be made in this country, and that would help to build up our home industries. The only other alternative is for the farmer not to produce his stuff. He has got to face one of two propositions, either our own people must buy more of his surplus products, which will be the case if we increase the consuming capacity of the home market, or he must stop growing those products. Now then the question for him to consider is, how much will it cost to secure that home market. The farmers recognize that the protective tariff now in force in this country is in their interest. We have no farmers' deputations down here asking for a reduction of the tariff. They are willing to submit to the present tariff in order to develop the. home market. But they have a right to ask themselves, recognizing the benefit of the home market: How much is it going to cost to secure immediately that home market ? That is the crux of this whole question. Now the opposition say : Put on a prohibitive tariff, that will do the business. It will also reduce the great revenue enjoyed by the government. They will no longer have occasion to quarrel with the Finance Minister if they introduce a prohibitory tariff as a remedy for our present ills. The Finance Minister will no longer be able to say that he has a surplus of $13,000,000. That evil, if it is one, will certainly be done away with. The present tariff, while it encourages the home market, also provides a revenue for the government and secures a paying market for home manufactures, and general prosperity for all. That is the stand taken by the government, and the farmers accept these conditions. Some manufacturers are content with the present conditions, while some want more protection than they now get. While I am not prepared to say which class is entitled to an increase in the tariff, I do believe	that there are industries in this country that are being injured by the preferential, that have been injured in the past from the want of a surtax on German goods ; and there are industries that are being injured by under-valuation from the United States. Those industries that are being made a slaughter market for American goods should be considered, and their welfare should be looked after by the government of this country. I believe that the government is now alive to the situation, and recognize that under-valuation has been taking place for a number of years. They are appointing more officials on the customs staff in order to prevent that evil, and they are getting the machinery into good working order. I know some industries that are likely to be closed up from this very evil of under-valuation. Still, we must admit that the manufacturers as a whole, with the exception of a few, are in a highly prosperous condition, there is no question of that. I believe that the government will be alert, and will be able to meet any changed conditions that present themselves. Ubelieve they will have to be on the alert for that slump which the manufacturers fear on the other side. We do not fear it in this country, because we have not got our money all invested in the business. But we have to realize the tremendous development that is taking place in manufacturing interests in the United States, the terrible trusts and combines that have been formed there, which are more powerful even than the Senate and House of Representatives. It behooves us to realize that one company controls $140,000,000 worth of capital ; that there are nearly two hundred trusts controlling over $3,500,000,000 of capital, and producing nearly $1,661,000,000 worth of goods ; that the manufacturers of the United States produce about $7.000.000,000 worth, nearly $8,000,000,000 worth of manufactured goods properly so-called, or $13,000,000,000 worth if you include the products of the hand trades and reduplications. If you take the hand trades alone they amount to $8,500,000,000, of which not 31 per cent, but 12 per cent, is exported to the markets of the world. We find that the product amounts now to $800,000,000 more than the people of the United States consume: They have agents the world over selling goods at less than it costs to produce them, recouping themselves in the highly protected markets at home in order that they may make sacrifices in the markets of the world. Our manufacturers say there is a danger. As soon as the consumption in the United States for these manufactured goods cease, the productive power, which will not cease, will go on producing, they must immediately find markets and the question which presents itself to their minds is this : Is the Canadian tariff high enough, under the conditions which are sure to obtain in a short period of time to preserve for us what we

have spent years in accumulating and in developing-the manufactories over which we have control ? No wonder that they are asking for an increase in the tariff. If I were a manufacturer and had the same interests at stake, I think I, myself, would shout for higher protection, louder than I am doing to-day, but, I have faith that the government that in 1896 assumed the helm of affairs and directed the ship of state to the haven of prosperity, are still able and willing when the conditions change, once more to listen to the voice of reason and to continue to guide that ship in the future as in the past along prosperous lines.
Now, there is one industry iu particular that we ought to feel thankful the government have done something for, though they have done very little for it. The binder twine industry is a peculiar industry, separate from all others and it bears a peculiar relation to the other industries of the country. It has to compete for trade in Canada alone against an organized body of twine manufacturers, which controls 90 per cent of the entire output of the United States. The International Harvester Company is the octopus that they have to fight against and against their onslaught they are absolutely powerless. Many people have been induced to go into the manufacture of binder twine. The hon. Minister of Finance stated the other day that many have gone into it, but they have gone into it under a false impression. They were under the impression that because the Brantford Binder Twine Company in three years earned dividends amounting to 200 per cent, all they had to do was to get a company of farmers to put their money into -the binder twine business and -they would likewise be able to declare dividends of 40 per cent, O') pe<- cent and 100 per cent. It is not always that we have manilla wars. It is not always that raw manilla jumps from 34, cents a pound to 13 cents a pound. A company has to have on hand a large quantity of raw material in order to enable it to make a profit of nearly $150,000 on the increase in the value of its raw material alone. That accounts for the 200 per cent dividends declared by the Brantford Binder Twine Company, but last year, in the face of a first class consuming demand in the North-west Territories it made 8 per cent, the Ontario Farmers Company made 5 per cent, the Consumers Cordage Company, which did not happen to have on hand $150,000 worth of raw product, has made 21 per cent-, per annum during the last seven years. The Chatham Binder Twine factory is closed up, and the Richelieu Cordage Company has closed its factory. Nearly all the binder twine factories in this country are owned by farmers who have gone into the business to prevent monopoly and that is the reason why the Farmers Binder Twine Company of Brantford was started. It has been successful because some 8,000 farmers be-Mr. HEYD.
came the agents and distributing centres for the institution. It costs the company nothing to sell its goods and it is able to keep on making binder twine. But the others are in dread. They do not know where they stand to-day. The United States market is closed against them by a duty of 45 per cent upon all binder twine of which manilla is a component part. With an octopus there controlling 90 per cent of the entire output, with the ability to begin in Texas and follow the markets up and when they reach the latter part of the season with a remnant of their supplies on hand, Canada is the dumping ground. The menace is not to the binder twine companies alone, but it is to the farmers of this country. The independent binder twine companies which we have in Canada are absolutely at the mercy of this foreign corporation which can charge what they like and when they like. The farmers of Canada are absolutely at their mercy if they have a glut of grain, as they are likely to have this year, that may reach to the producing power of the binder twine companies, and when they come to take the crop from -the golden wheat fields they may find themselves left in the lurch for want of binder twine. The binder twine manufacturers met members of the government. They said :	If you will give
us a protection of 124 per cent on binder twine we will undertake to produce all the people of Canada want. We have producing power sufficient to meet the requirements of the Canadian consumers. We will agree to fix our price at the price quoted by the International Harvester Company to the people of the* United States and if we exceed their price you shall have the power by Order in Council to wipe out the duty so as to prevent us from getting a monopoly or extorting money from the consumers of the country. A proposition of that kind may be very difficult to deal with. Our farmer friends do not realize the importance of this question. We have the ability to make binder twine in Canada to-day. We have -the factories, we have the labour to make all this country demands and we will make it and sell it to the consuming public as cheaply as the International Harvester Company sell It to the people of the United States, if we have a certain amount of tariff for revenue applied to the binder twine industry. It is these industries which are being injured that I have the greatest solicitude for. It is not the establishments that are developing and increasing beyond all reason. It is -those that are being injured and which do not know what to do. They do not know what to do because the price of manilla had not until recently even been fixed. If it should turn out that they have too much binder twine in the United States there is nothing to prevent the International Harvester Company from saying that) the price in Canada shall be 12 cents per pound. Our price is 13 cents. The price

of pure raauilla is 13 cents. But, to suit their own purposes the price of the International Harvester Conqiany can he put down to 10 cents per pound for the purpose of wiping out every binder twine industry we have in this country. They are at the mercy of the trust. I would make it a little harder for the International Harvester Company to sell their goods in Canada. I would like binder twine to contribute by a revenue duty to the coffers of this country. Why should they have been singled out. If a revenue duty is the policy of the government it should apply to binder twine as well as to reapers and to mowers.
Now, Sir, I hear already that some industries that have been subjected to the preference; some that have been subjected to the slaughter, are being hard hit. I have letters from some which say that it may force them to close up. I have one letter from the Cutlery Company, who think they will not be able to wait until the government finds out whether Great Britain is going to give us a preference or the United States reciprocity. They cannot wait another year and fight against the present conditions. There are many industries in that position, and I do hope, and I hope with confidence, that the present condition will not last much longer; and that those people who have been hoping against hope as the binder twine people have been for five or six years, will be relieved from the tension to which they have been subjected, and at least put upon the plane that is occupied by the ordinary manufacturers of this country. I trust, Sir, that when this slump which is sure to come, manifests itself, the government will be on the alert, and if specific duties are needed or if anything else is needed to secure the manufacturers of this country from that invasion, they should be so secured. It is my opinion, Sir, that cheap goods to the consumer for a year or two, will never pay Canada for the loss of these magnificent manufacturing industries that have developed so wondrously during the last few years and are to-day the pride of this great Dominion of Canada.

I listened to the lengthy speech of the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) and I was not surprised that the Speaker had to draw his attention to the fact that he was not keeping to the amendment before the House. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) said in answer to Mr. Speaker, that he had not read the amendment, but even that ignorance of the subject did not deter the hon. gentleman from criticising the leader of the opposition for promulgating a policy which he (Mr. Davis) had to admit he knew nothing about. Well, Sir, the policy of the Conservative party is adequate protection for home industries. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) told us that he could not understand the term ' adequate protection,' because it was not definite enough. As to that, it may liot be amiss for me to give him the authority of a gentleman of high standing in this House; a. gentleman whom he has supported for the last few years; a gentleman who stood so high in the estimation of the Reform party that he was selected by the l'riine Minister to take the most responsible portfolio in his government when he came to power in 1896.
I refer to the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). Let me in the first place read the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition. It is :
This House regarding the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at all times secure the Canadian market for Canadians ;
And that the financial policy of the government should include a measure for the thorough and judicious readjustment of the tariff at the present session
Now, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) does not understand that, let me read to him what the Hon. Mr. Tarte said about it the other evening, and perhaps that may illuminate the mind of the member for Saskatchewan. The Hon. Mr. Tarte said :
Let me compliment the hon. the leader of the opposition on the speech he has delivered:	On both sides of the House it is admitted to be one of the ablest utterances that have been made on the question of a tariff in this parliament. It is delightful to hear questions of that importance discussed in such an able manner. His motion has the right ring.
That illustrates the difference between the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) and the member for St. Mary's, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte). Let me say further, Mr. Speaker, that there Is a demand from the people of the North-west for local self-government as we have it in the other provinces of the Dominion. Travelling through the territories last fall, I found that Liberals and Conservatives were agreed that the time had come when they should have local selfgovernment. And, is it not a surprise that a gentleman coming from the territories as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) does, should have addressed the House for two long hours and make no reference whatever to this all-

important question to the people of his constituency. On this subject let me quote what the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said in 1893-not since the Liberals came into power but before they came into power, and that makes a great deal of difference with these gentlemen. Referring to the $277,000 that the Conservative government was voting in 1895 for the North-west Territories Mr. Charlton said :
We could save the whole of that expense by* allowing the North-west Territory people to manage their own concerns. Give them selfgovernment, do not lead them around as infants with a string, but let them manage their own business like free British subjects.
What does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) think about the condition of things now ? Does he think that because the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) advocated free trade on agricultural implements and now favours a revenue tariff of 20 per cent on them, that this same hon. gentleman will give his adhesion to anything which the government proposes ?
I listened with some pleasure to the speech of the member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd), but I am unable yet to determine whether he is a protectionist or a free trader. I could not make out whether he was advocating a revenue tariff or protection; probably he was arguing for both. But for the information of the House let me quote something the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) said last year and which is to be found in ' Hansard,' page 299. He said :
I am in favour of increasing the protection on the woollen industry of this country.
Notwithstanding that he held this opinion last year, he is ready to stand up in the House to-day and to support the existing tariff, and to say that he is in favour of a revenue tariff, and to say further that the present tariff is all right. Why did he not tell his leader this year that he was in favour of increasing the protection of the woollen industries of this country. Again, he said last year :
I am willing to protect even to the extent of extreme protection.
What has changed his mind since. Further he said :
I am opposed to any kind of reciprocity with the people of the United States.
This is what he said last year, but to-dav he stood on the floor of the House to tell us, that he warned the government that the day is coming when the British market will in some measure be closed to us and that we will not be able to supply it to the extent that we are supplying it at the present moment. What does he ask ? He says the government is called upon to provide a home market for the farmers. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman, or the government themselves, how it is possible to have an increased home market without having increased Mr. BLAIN.
manufacturing establishments ? Every man knows that it is an utter impossibility.
The hon. Finance Minister, in his budget speech in the session of 1901, stated that he believed in a policy of stability of tariffs. The right hon. Prime Minister has made the same statement on several occasions. That is their policy as a government and a party. I think it is a very good text for the people of any country, so far as it can be lived up to. Would it not be well for us to look into this government's record to see if they have lived up to that splendid text ? The Liberal-Conservative party were defeated in 1890 ; the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power and formed his government ; and at the session of 1897 that government introduced what they called the Fielding tariff, and announced to the world : We present this to the people of Canada as a stable tariff ; stability of tariffs is our watchword. That tariff was adopted in 1897 ; but how long did these hon. gentlemen live up to their doctrine of stability of tariffs ? Not very long, for in the following session, that of 1S98, the hon. Finance Minister stood up in his place in the House and said to the manufacturing industries and to the people of Canada : We are going to alter the tariff and make a radical change. What was the change ? He announced a preferential reduction to British goods of 121 per cent; nay, it was supposed to be world-wide. How long did that last ? Not very long. In the next session, in 1899, the hon. Finance Minister again stood up in his place and announced another reduction. I suppose he said, discussing it in the Cabinet; This tariff is not satisfactory yet; we will have to forget that stable tariff doctrine, and put away the 12* per cent preference to goods coming to this country from England, and adopt a 25 per cent preference. And he announced that change in the House. Stability of tariff, do you say ? In the meantime, the manufacturers came to the government and said : We cannot continue our manufacturing if you continue this reduction of the tariff. Yet in the next session they came along with another sweeping change. They said : We will put away that 25 per cent preference and adopt a 331 per cent preference on goods coming from England. Would you call that a stable tariff ? Would it be called a stable tariff by men intending coming to this country to engage in agricultural or manufacturing pursuits ? Not a bit of it. In 1897 the government looked for something further. They said : There is to be a large development in the railways of Canada, and we will adopt some legislation to enable steel rails to be manufactured in this country. In November, 1900, just before the general election, the government sat down in Council and entered into a contract with the Clergue Company of Sault Ste. Marie, not by open Act of parliament, but by a special secret contract, given without competition,

to supply the government with 125,000 tons of steel rails. The contract was to extend over a period of five years. I heard the Finance Minister stand np in his place in the House and say : We are having a splendid steel rail industry established in the province from which X come, and it will soon be in operation. But that contract was not lived up to-why ? Because it was made in secret. Every man in this country should have had an opportunity of tendering for those steel rails. Speaking for myself, I am opposed to this kind of class legislation. Coming to the session of 1902 and keeping before our minds that promise to the people of Canada of a stable tariff, we had a discussion of the tariff in this House. The lion. ex-Mi'nister of Putoliq Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) the other evening, referring to the statement made by the lion. Minister of Finance on that occasion, said :
Last year my hon. friend the Minister o' Finance in his budget speech said that he would not revise the tariff that session, because there were reasons why he should not do so-the census returns of manufactures were not available, and the London conference was on ; but the words ot the hon. Minister of Finance, which I read in the House on another occasion, conveyed to the country the impression that the tariff would be revised this year. The business men of the country took those words as a pledge for a revision of the tariff at this present session. The words of the Finance Minister of last year were a great deal more definite on that point than his words of this year. Last year my hon. friend did not argue on principle against a revision of the tariff, hut we realize that conditions have arisen in the world that will make it necessary for us to revise the tariff at some future day. These words, I say, were understood to mean a revision this year. I can appeal to the business men of the country-they took the words of the hon. gentleman as a promise. I know that there are in Ontario and the province of Quebec several industries which cannot live under the present tariff, and there is one thing that surprises me. This Liberal side of the House is empty to-night. I would like to see it full. Bub what surprises me is that there are so many members of parliament on this side who have told us that they share my views, who have written me and told me repeatedly that they share my views, and who have not been able to impress their views on the Liberal party. I say it openly, I say it from the bottom of my heart, that I fully expected that the Liberal party, with which I have been connected during the last ten years, would carry out the policy it was understood in 1896 they would carry out. I am weighing my words. I know what arrangement, what understanding took place between some public men. I know what took place. I do not divulge any secrets. I know w'hat we did in the election of 1896 in Montreal. I see within the radius of my eye public men who, at our request, came to the city of Montreal, went to the manufacturers, with the knowledge of the leaders of their party, and told them not only would the tariff not be disturbed, but it would be changed in the right direction when the proper time came. There was no secret about that. I shall not give names. There are men who hear me-I
am sorry there are not more on those benches -who know' that I am perfectly right. I am out of office because I could not stay in office under the present circumstances.
What do hon. gentlemen think of that kind of a statement ? Is that a statement which should be made on behalf of a government that advocates stability of tariff ? What are we to think of hon. gentlemen, who advocate a policy of tariff stability, going secretly to the manufacturers, prior to the general elections, and saying to them : ' You need not be disturbed about our utterances. True, we have advocated reciprocity ; true we have promised free trade; but do not be alarmed, we tell you in secret-because we do many things in secret-that if the tariff be changed at all, it will be changed in the interest of the manufacturer.' Is it a matter for surprise that when we find a government, which pronounced itself in favour of stability of tariff, making important changes in that tariff every session, so that no one can tell exactly what may happen next, our capitalists and manufacturers should refuse to invest in manufacturing industries. This session the government have introduced a new feature into their so-called policy of tariff stability. They have inposed a surtax on goods from Germany. Well, Mr. Speaker, in my humble opinion such legislation is anything but wise and prudent statesmanship. I do not wish to be misunderstood. In saying this, I do not wish to be understood as being opposed to increased protection ? On the contrary, I am in favour of increasing protection to all our Canadian industries which require it. But at the same time, I do not think that it is wise or politic to single out any special country and say to that country: ' You shall not bring in your goods under the ordinary tariff, but you shall pay one-third more than the rates charged other countries.' If for no other such a policy is impolitic and inadvisable for this reason. We have in this country a large German settlement. We have particularly in the central part of Ontario-in Waterloo and in the surrounding district-many German settlers who are among the most prosperous and enterprising citizens to be found in this Dominion. We are inviting the surplus population of Germany to come in and settle on our unoccupied lands. We are holding out great inducements to good citizens from every part of the world to cast their lot in with us. But when a German immigrant takes up a location in bur Northwest, what will happen ? He may find beside him a Russian and along side the Russian a settler from some other foreign country, and when he takes up our tariff he will be confronted by this fact ; that goods from every foreign country in the world except Germany are admitted on the same basis, but on German goods a special tax is imposed, and that is a condition of affairs which will naturally excite his resentment and prejudice him against the

laws and institutions of his newly adopted country. That is why I am opposed to this policy of discrimination against the goods of any particular country. What I maintain is that the government should look carefully into the subject of imports from Germany, and if it came to the conclusion that the goods we import from that country could be and should be manufactured in Canada, then it would be perfectly justified, in the interests of this country, in making its tariff sufficiently high to keep out such imports and similar imports from every country in the world. But I do not think that it is wise to apply any special tariff to any one foreign country which is not equally applicable to every other.
My hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) spoke a good deal about the farmers. He pleaded both for and against them. He argued that it was in the interests of the people that we should have protection, but he immediately proceeded to warn the people against too high protection. He at first said that our imports from the United States did not hurt us and then he dwelt on the necessity of our imposing a higher tariff on some American products, especially barb wire and binder twine. Bet me refer to that binder twine question. When we had a Liberal-Conservative government in power, that government put a duty of 124 per cent on binder twine imported into Canada, no matter from what country. The Reform party took issue with the Liberal-Conservatives in that tariff and claimed that, in the interests of the Canadian farmer, binder twine should be admitted free. If that were done, they said that our farmers would purchase their binder twine at cheaper rates. They applied the same argument to barbwire, which was protected by the Liberal-Conservative government. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Reform party came into power and took the duty off binder twine and barb-wire. This gave the Canadian people an opportunity to compare the results of the two policies. What has been the .result of taking off the duty ? Why, the result has been that every year since then we have had a large quantity of binder twine and barbwire manufactured by foreigners coming into this country and sold to our Canadian farmers at higher rates than formerly were the rule, when these two industries enjoyed the advantage of protection. And we have today that devoted Liberal, my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd), lifting up his hand and appealing to have the tariff raised again because at this moment our binder twine factories are closed down.
Which of the two great parties, Mr. Speaker, are entitled to the support and confidence of the farmers of Canada ? Both sides are in accord on this point, that our farming community is the most important in this country. I am one of those who believe that the farmers of Canada can be protected.

I shall read just one or two paragraphs from this letter. He says :

class, in that large sums are paid annually for all barrel material.
Many works are shut down and capital unproductive owing to the present conditions of the tariff. There is ample capacity to supply the requirements of the Dominion if Canadian salt makers were permitted to have possession of their own rightful market.

There is a duty on salt imported from the United States of 5 cents per 100 pounds in bulk and 74 cents per 100 pounds in packages.
There is a duty imposed on salt going into the United States of 8 cents per 100 pounds in bulk and 12 cents per 100 pounds in packages.
There is no duty on salt imported into this country from any other source than the United States.
The imports of salt from Mediterranean pons and Great Britain amount approximately to an average of 100,000 tons or 700,000 barrels per annum.
The annual consumption of salt in Canada may be calculated at 1,000,000 barrels or 150,000 tons.
Practically two-thirds of the market is therefore filled with foreign made salt admitted with the package entirely free of duty.
He says in conclusion :
In view of the foregoing it is asked that a duty similar to that existing in the United States be imposed on all salt coming into Canada, viz.: 8 cents per 100 pounds in bulk and 12 cents per 100 pounds in packages.
That illustrates the condition of a large number of manufacturing establishments in this country that are suffering under the present tariff. The woollen industry is suffering. My hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) has stated that the binder twine industry is suffering. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the cotton industry is suffering. The farmers are suffering in many instances because there is not a higher protective tariff on their produce. I should like to make one further statement on the farming question. There were in 1879, duties placed on butter, cheese and eggs coming into this country. These items have been protected continuously whether the Liberal Conservative party were in office or the Keform party were in office. These three industries that are entirely farming industries have been protected ever since 1879, and I wish to say, and I make this statement on high authority, that there is no animal in this country considering its value, that produces so much profit for the farmers as the hen. The egg producing industry, the cheese industry and the butter industry that have been protected continuously by both political parties all these long years are in a prosperous condition. The farmers of Canada are supplying the butter that is used by the people of Canada. The fanners of Canada are supplying the cheese that is used by the people of Canada, and the farmers of Canada are supplying the eggs that are consumed by the people of Canada. Now, a considerable quantity of these commodities come in un-

der the present tariff, from the United States, and I submit that adequate protection should be applied to these articles, that in accordance with the principles enunciated in the amendment moved by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) the tariff should be placed sufficiently high so. that the United States farmers could not send to this country one dollar's worth of these goods in competition with the product of our own farmers. In conclusion I wish to say that I am in favour of the amendment submitted by the hon. leader of the opposition, that I believe in a higher protective tariff for the industries of this country, that I think the market gardeners and the farmers of Canada should have received better treatment at the hands of this government than a promise, that I am in favour of and will support legitimate and adequate protection for the farming industry, for the manufacturing industry, on every article that can be grown on Canadian farms and on every article that can be manufactured by the Canadian people. That is the policy I am prepared to support. I will support it if it comes from the Liberal side of the House, and I will support it if it comes from this side of the House. So soon as a resolution is introduced into this House adopting protection that will measure up to the standard I have laid down, I will stand up in my place and support that resolution, because I think it is in the best interests of the farmers of the county I have the honour to represent, and in the best interests of the people of Canada from one end of the country to the other.
