Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the discussion on the amendment, and on the budget propositions that have been presented. I would like to state my position in regard to the amendment by congratulating the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) on the fact that his budget, as presented, turned down fairly and squarely the insolent and absurd demand made a few days before the session opened by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for the application of a prohibitive tariff to Canada. I may say when the campaign on behalf of this demand was in progress during the past year, the result was looked to with some degree of doubt. It may be said that those who doubted had not proper confidence in the minister, or in the ministry. But there are many sides to the question and when it is remembered that the minister has always been careful not to take an extreme position on the tariff ; that he has always held that the tariff is rather a compromise than a finality ; that it does not, as did the tariff of the preceding government, represent the acme of human wisdom ; and when besides and beyond that it is remembered that this Mr. BLAIN.
association was actively organized for the express purpose of forcing tariff concessions, backed as they claim by some $400,000,000 of capital, and being in a position to enforce their demand if such demands could be enforced, it was not wonderful if we should look for some changes and some effort to satisfy these gentlemen to a degree. I say, Sir, that it is with extreme satisfaction the country has heard that these demands have not been acceded to in any degree; and that the tariff stands,to-day, without concession, as it did a year ago. I do not claim, nor is it claimed by any one, that the tariff is perfect, that any tariff can be perfect; or that changed conditions do not necessitate from time to time changes in the tariff. We all agree to that, but when a' straight demand, a bulldozing demand was made upon the government for concessions which in my humble estimation at any rate, and I believe in the estimation of the large majority of the people of this country were absolutely unreasonable, it is a satisfaction that they simply were not acceded to in any part. It was the only answer that could properly be given ; it was the answer that was given, and the government is to be congratulated upon that answer. I believe that had there been any tampering with the general tariff at this session-I say this for the information of the government-I believe that had there been any tampering with the tariff at this session looking towards increases, it would have been taken by the country at large as a surrender on the part of the government to those demands of the manufacturing association, and that there would have been created a lack of confidence on the part of their friends towards the government that would have had serious if not actually disastrous results.
While we have to congratulate the minister upon the stand taken in regard to these demands, it appears to me, however, that throughout the course of this debate, there has been a lack of appreciation of the respective magnitude of the various interests involved. I do not know whether the government is in danger of being finally stampeded into a policy of protection by the continual outcry that is made from, not only the other side of the House but also from this side of the House. But it may not be out of order in any case for me at this stage of the debate to present in some degree the case for the Canadian consumer, who seems to have been entirely forgotten up to the present moment.
We have heard of this, and that, and the other industry which is suffering for more protection. Now, for my part. I am a protectionist ; I believe thoroughly in protection. I am no theoretical free trader. I believe that it is the business of the government of the country to take any means that may be necessary to advance the interests of the country whether it be by tariff adjustment or by any other means. The dif-

ference between myself and the gentlemen wTho have already . spoken here on this subject seems to. be, that they recognize a high tariff as the only method of protection, and they recognize the manufacturing industry as the only interest that is worthy of protection. I decline to accept the proposition that high tariff is the only method of protection, and I much more strongly deny the proposition that the manufacturing industry is the only one worthy of protective consideration. What proportion does the manufacturing industry of Canada bear to the other industries of Canada ? If we take the exports of Canada we find :	That the mines export
$10,000,000; the fisheries, $10,000,000; the forests, $21,000,000 ; agriculture, $93,000,000; and manufactures, $1S,000,000. We find that by the last census the population of Canada was in the neighbourhood of 5.000,000, and the number of people actually employed in what are generally considered to be manufactures, amounted to about 100,000. Now, as a large number of those who ore employed in manufactures are not adults, it would not be fair to give the usual count of five persons dependent upon each operative ; but allowing four, it would appear that there were about 400,000, people out of our population of 5,000,000 who are directly interested in manufactures, or practically one individual as compared with nine individuals interested in the other industries of the country. I say that any legislation which looks to the protection or the advantage of the interests in which only one-tenth of the people are concerned, ignoring the interests and advantage of the nine-tenths, is not properly a policy of protection. It will be conceded by all, that those industries of the country which are the exporting industries, the price of whose product is necessarily regulated by the export market are not susceptible of benefit from a protective tariff to anything like the same degree that is an industry whose prices are regulated by the home demand rather than by the export price. You can, by raising the duty, raise the price of a manufactured article, so long as that article depends chiefly on the home market for its consumption. You cannot raise the price by increasing the duty on an article whose price chiefly depends upon the export market. That is the position as it exists as between the manufacturing industry and those other creative industries of the country, and the policy which undertakes to advantage the one-tentli at the expense of the nine-tenths is a policy which cannot be recognized as a protective tariff, and which I do not think this country at this time and in its present condition will recognize as a protective policy. We have no quarrel with the manufacturers of Canada ; we have no wish other than they should prosper. Our objection is that the manufacturers of Canada desire to prosper by reason of tariff adjustment rather than by reason of
their own exertions, energy and ability. We who depend on agriculture are left to our own resources. We must necessarily maintain our position in the markets of the world, let those markets be high or low, and all we ask is that the manufacturing industries be left in the same position approximately. It was said by the preceding speaker that the agricultural industry is protected. I think the hon. leader of the opposition said the same thing. They both want it to be more protected, and they, argue that those who do not believe in a high tariff should declare for no tariff at all on agricultural products. Would they please remember that, in the first place, the tariff does not exist for the puprose of protecting any industry.

subtopic: TOTAL EXPORTS OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS AND ANIMALS AND THEIR PRODUCTS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will pardon me, I think he expressed himself on one occasion in favour of a duty on oats, saying that it had a good effect in protecting the western farmer. I remember seeing an article of that kind in the very able journal over which he presides.

subtopic: TOTAL EXPORTS OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS AND ANIMALS AND THEIR PRODUCTS.
speechtext: I intend to come to that. These hon. gentlemen argue that as we are not in favour of a high tariff, we should therefore hold that there should be no tariff on agricultural products. Now, the tariff is imposed for the purpose of raising a revenue by customs taxes, and there is no reason why that revenue should not be raised by a tariff on agricultural products as well as on anything else. There is no reason why the farmers should not have the benefit of the incidental protection which results from! a revenue tariff. That is all the protection the farming industry has, and we certainly demand our share of that incidental protection. But while that is true as regards agricultural products in isolated cases, it1 does not apply to the general output of agriculture. On the great export products of wheat, cattle, butter, eggs and poultry, a protective tariff is practically of no use at all in the way of increasing prices. Do my hon. friends deny that ? Do they say that the agricultural duties do increase the general prices of these products to the farmers ?

subtopic: TOTAL EXPORTS OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS AND ANIMALS AND THEIR PRODUCTS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me ? I think that may be answered by the course of the government in makiug a reduction in the duties on corn and wheat and corn meal.

speechtext: I was not asking about the policy of the: government. I was asking the question of the opposition.

speechtext: That answers the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: TOTAL EXPORTS OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS AND ANIMALS AND THEIR PRODUCTS.
speechtext:
I do not want that answer. I want the answer from the opposition, not from the government. If they could advance the prices of agricultural products by increasing the duties, why did they not, during the agricultural depression which existed

previous to 1890, increase those duties and thereby increase the prices of the fanners' products ? Either they were not able to increase the prices by increasing the duties, or they were not willing to. They can adopt which inference they like. If they were able to and did not, they were nut friends of the farmers; and if they were not able to, they should not stand before this House and claim that it is possible to increase the prices of agricultural products by increasing the duties.
Our position, then, as representing agriculture, is this :	We accept the position as
to raising the duties by means of a revenue tariff. Having accepted that position, we are entitled to such a measure of incidental protection as is afforded by a revenue tariff, and we demand that every other industry in the country shall be put on the same footing. That is where we take issue with our friends of the Manufacturers'Association.
Just what does the demand of this Manufacturers Association amount to ? There may be people who imagine that it is simply a demand to revert to the so-called national policy tariff of 1878. But there was all the difference in the world between the so-called national policy of 1878, and the demand of the Manufacturers' Association. The national policy of 1878 was placed before the country on the plea that the manufacturers needed assistance-that if they were given assistance, it would benefit the country at large, and that in the end the prices of manufactured goods would come down. The demand of the Manufacturers' Association is that the tariff shall be raised for the purpose of preventing goods from coming in. It is not the demand of an industry that wants assistance; it is the demand of an industry which, having grown and become strong, demands to be relieved from competition. In 1878 it was a request to help the manufacturers, in order that the country might be helped; but the demand of to-day is that the manufacturers shall be protected so that, no matter what happens to the country, they will be all right. That is the position put before the House by lion, gentlemen opposite during this debate. 1 think it was the hon. leader of the opposition who argued that, as we see hard times ahead of us, when; Canada may become a slaughter market for imported manufactured goods, we want a prohibitive tariff against those times. On what grounds of justice do the manufacturers make this demand ? When the hard times come, the purchasing power of the people is decreased. Are they then to be compelled, under stress of a" tariff law, to pay more for the goods they shall have to buy, in order that our friends the manufacturers shal be lifted above the general depression ? I hope not. I do not agree with any such contention. I think that of all the unreasonable demands that have been made on behalf of the manufacturers, that is the most unreasonable. We are willing that they should share with Mr. OLIVER.
us in the general prosperity, but we ask that they should also share with us in the general adversity when it conies. When we have only 50 cents to buy a dollars worth of the goods we require, we do not want them to be placed in a position to charge us a dollar for only 50 cents worth of goods.

speechtext: I am sorry to say that I cannot allow it to stand over until next week, because the promoters of this railway are already hard at work in the interests of the company. There is a survey going on and the works will be started shortly during this session and besides I may inform my hon. friend that this afternoon I was told by the hon. member from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) who takes a deep interest in this Bill that he did not intend to make any objection to its being reported and read the third time.

subtopic: PRIVATE BILLS.
subsubtopic: ATLANTIC QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I wish to explain why I do not raise any objection to this Bill as now framed. My instructions were first to oppose the Bill because the promoters intended constructing the road through the interior of Gaspe, some sixty or seventy miles from the shore, which would not suit the people of that country, who live almost exclusively along the shore. Both the Quebec and Dominion governments have expended a million and a half dollars to help in the construction of the Baie de Chaleurs railway, which extends 100 miles from Metapedia down to Paspe-biac. Public interest requires that this road should be completed before another road is undertaken through the interior of the peninsula, where as yet there is no population. It was my intention to oppose the Bill before the House if the company had not bound itself to build the shore line concurrently with their line in the interior. The Quebec legislature granted a charter two years ago and revived it this month, so that the company could proceed with its work, in the interior regardless of any legislation here. But in view of the fact that it is willing to build the shore line at the same time as the line through the interior, I have concluded that there

is no objection to the measure. The conditions are most reasonable. The company has to build ten miles of its road from the terminus of the Atlantic and the Lake Superior railway within one year, or else its charter will lapse for both the shore line and the line through the interior. It is a fair compromise in the interest of both Bonaventure and Gaspe counties. The peninsula has been sadly in need of railways for many years. The change in the policy of the government about 1SS4 prevented the people there having the railway which they might have had if the original Baie de Ohaleurs road had been constructed as part and parcel of the Intercolonial Railway instead of being handed over to a private railway company, and we would have been spared the long series of scandals connected with the Baie de Cha-leurs road. At present the English bondholders are in possession of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway, the company having transferred to them the road on account of its inability to pay the interest on the bonds. Had the trustees of that company come forward with a reasonable proposition and undertaken to continue the Shore line, L would have given them the preference. But, in the absence of any such proposition, and in view of the fact that there are 8300,000 owing by the company to the farmers and labourers in the county of Bonaventure, the only option left me was to give the Atlantic, Quebec and Western Railway Company a fair chance.

subtopic: PRIVATE BILLS.
subsubtopic: ATLANTIC QUEBEC AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I concur in the remarks of my hon. friend from Bonaventure. If the promoters of this company had agreed to build only the line through the interior,
I myself, as representing the county of Gaspe, would not have supported the Bill. But I induced the company to add to its Bill a clause in the nature of a compromise, by which the company is obliged to extend its railway from Gaspe Basin at the extremity of the peninsula as far as the terminus of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company. This company has given further evidence of its bona fides. During the last two months it has made a complete survey of the interior and the reports so far are most favourable. The survey of the interior line is now completed and Mr. O'Sullivan, a well known surveyor from the province of Quebec is now en route to survey the coast line from Gaspe Basin to Paspebiac. I am pleased to say that within one year from the sanction of this Act we will have at least ten miles and perhaps more, constructed along the shores -of Gaspd and the county of Bonaventure. This Bill, has given rise to some discussion in the press and I am sorry to say that those who wrote in the newspapers were far from being well informed. This Bill represents public opinion in the county of Gaspe and Bonaventure and I shall not attempt to inflict on the House a reading of the numerous petitions
which I hold in my hand. But, I may say that, with the amendment suggested by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Mareil), to which I have agreed, and which I seconded with pleasure in the Railway Committee, a new era has dawned on the county of Gaspf: and the county of Bonaventure.

It seems to me that these are unusual proceedings. Judging from what you have read, Mr. Chairman, so much has been added to the Bill, or so many changes have been made, that, in all fairness to the House, the Bill should have been reprinted, so that we might have an opportunity of studying the changes proposed. I presume there are very few members, perhaps not more than two or three, who really have any intelligent knowledge of the character of this legislation. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) who, no doubt, has more special knowledge on this subject than the rest of us on this side of the House, has made a request that the Bill should lie over. I think it is only reasonable that that request should be acceded to in order that we may have some person to speak for us with respect to these changes. I would not raise any objection to hurrying this Bill through the House were it not for the fact that no person is here to represent the government in this matter. I regard it as the duty of the Minister of Railways to be in his place when private Bills of this character are being passed through tlieir various stages, so that we may appeal to him and ascertain whether lie has pronounced upon the Bills and whether. in the opinion of his department they ought to pass. The minister is absent, and

there is no one here to represent him or to represent the Department of Railways and Canals. We are in utter ignorance as to the character of this legislation, and this is especially true since the Bill has been altered to such a very large extent as would appear from the amendments you have read. I think that, in the absence of the bon. member for Jacques Cartier, we are entitled to express the desire that the Bill should be laid over. The delay will be very slight and no inconvenience, so far as I can see, will result. I understand the measure would come up again ou Monday. I think it is only fair that this request should be acceded to that we may have an opportunity of studying the proposed amendments and dealing with the Bill on its merits. Otherwise we may regret that the Bill was allowed to go through in this hasty way. There may be wonderful revelations. We have heard a great deal about this railway. The old Baie des Chaleurs Railway once created a great sensation in this House. In fact we look with a great deal of suspicion on anything^ connected with railways down in Gaspe. I think it was well that the members of the House should have every opportunity of informing themselves before this legislation is allowed to go through. I again ask the leader of the House to consent to granting the request of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.
