When tlie House rose at six o'clock, I was making a comparison between the requests made in 1878 and the demand made in 1903 by the manufacturers of Canada. That which was in 1878 a request, became in 1903 a demand. The plea that was then made for assistance to a struggling industry has now become a threat on behalf of a self styled dominant interest. What was asked in'the general interest in 1878 is demanded in a special interest in 1903. The difference between the request of 1878 and the demand of 1903 is just as wide as the difference between the conditions prevailing then and now. And it is just as well that we should recognize the difference in those conditions, so that we may appreciate the injustice of the present demand. The promises that were made to justify the request for increased protection were the retaining of our population at home, the increase of our general wealth and prosperity, and the lowering of the price of manufactured products. At the end of eighteen years' experience of that policy, carried out by those who had every opportunity to put it to the test in its entirety, what has been the result ? Although during those eighteen years we had a national expenditure of six and a half million dollars per year over the national revenue, although we had the building up of a number of millionaires in the country, at the end of that period we found ourselves in a condition of commercial and industrial stagnation. Contrast that with our present position. To-day, after an experience of some seven years of a change of policy and a change of tariff, we have a prosperity in trade, commerce and finance such as this country never before .dreamed of. In 1878 we were asked to give protection to the manufacturers because they and the country were not prosperous. Now these manufacturers ai-e demanding more pro-

tection because they and the country are prosperous. In 1S78 they asked for protection because they needed it. Now they demand protection because the country is rich enough to stand it. The moral of this is that the manufacturers have thriven because the country has prospered-that the manufacturers depend on the farmers, and not the farmers on the manufacturers. We had eighteen year^ of effort to make the country prosperous by protecting the manufacturers, and that experiment resulted in dismal failure. We have had since then seven years' endeavour to make the country prosperous by increasing the facilities for agriculture and trade generally, and we find both the country and manufacturers prosperous to a degree they never were before. All of which shows that the policy of restriction produced the result that should naturally have been expected. In 1878 we voted for restriction of trade. During eighteen years we carried out that policy, and at the end of the eighteen years we had the natural result. In 1896 we voted for expansion of trade, and, for seven years we have had an increase of commerce, an increase of industry and prosperity. And to-day we are asked, practically, as it appears to me, to commit commercial, industrial and financial suicide, by reverting to the conaitlons which failed in the period from 1878 to 1896, and which, I believe, will fail again if the attempt is made to revert to them. It is the highest tribute that can be paid to the policy of protection to manufacturer's at the expense of the community, to the policy of building up tariff walls and restricting trade, to say that it was in the highest degree successful and that trade was restricted. The fact that the country was not prosperous was entirely another matter, and did not affect the theory or the success of the experiment. Just as with the surgeon who performs a very difficult operation, is able to announce that it was very successful; adding, as a mere detail that the patient died.
Now, as to the policy of a prohibitive tariff, there can be only one opinion from the standpoint of those who have to bear the burden of that tariff. I suppose there is only one opinion from the standpoint of those who get the benefit of it-that we take for granted. Among those who have to bear the burden of it there certainly should be, and reasonably can be, only one opinion. As those who are to have the benefit constitute only one-tenth of the community, and those who are to bear the burden constitute nine-tenths, it seems to me only one answer is to be given to such the demand for such a tariff from the standpoint of the welfare of the nation. The fact that the demand comes from both sides of the House, to a certain degree does not affect the condition at all. I would like to say to the Minister of Finance that, however, desirable it may be to
please everybody, that is beyond the limit of success ; but that the effort to please everybody generally results in pleasing nobody. If I understand what liberalism means, it stands for progress, but it stands for principle as much as it does for progress. Liberalism stands for principle, or it stands for nothing, and if it shall ever be that the impression goes abroad that Liberalism has become mere opportunism, then, no more can the Liberal party expect, and no more will it receive, the confidence of an intelligent and progressive country. I give all credit to the government for having withstood these demands, these united demands of the Manufacturers' Association -these dangerous demands, demands which, if acceded to, mean, as I contend, commercial and financial ruin to this country. And as these demands have not been acceded to, I take it for granted that the government must face the absolute, unquestioning and determined hostility of that same Manufacturers' Association and of every interest which they can bring to bear in their support. I take it for granted that the fight is on, as a matter of fact, between the present government and those interests which stand for a high tariff, whether they are in one province or the other and whether they call themselves Liberals or Conservatives. I, therefore, give the government all credit for the stand they have taken and for liav-iug accepted the challenge which was thrown down. But, for fear that there might be any misunderstanding with those of us who represent portions of the country the industries of which are not susceptible of successful and profitable protection, I will go a little further and will challenge some of the propositions laid down in the budget speech.
I said a while ago that I was a protectionist. Beyond that, I believe in retaliation. But, I believe in retaliation only as a measure of self-defence, and when you are sure of hurting the other fellow more than you hurt yourself. Now, I am not so sure, on looking into the matter a little carefully, that our proposed retaliation against Germany is altogether favourable to ourselves. I notice that that policy rvas applauded on both sides of the House, and particularly on the other side. Perhaps if we look into the matter a little carefully, Ave shall not see quite so much reason for applause. Looking over the Trade and Navigation iteturns, to-day I found that Ave imported last year 371,000.000 pounds of sugar, at a value of about 87,500,000, upon which the duty would amount to about 82,750,000. The duty on the low grade sugar is 621 cents per hundred pounds, and on the high grade it is 81.25 per hundred pounds. I found that we imported from Germany about 183,500,000 pounds of sugar, about half of our total import, of the value of about 835.000.000. the duty on which was about 81.750,000. If we import an equal

1S20
amount of sugar from Germany next year under that retaliatory system which was so strongly applauded on both sides, but particularly on the other side, we shall pay into our treasury an additional amount of $445,000 over the amount paid in last ; year. This, perhaps, will change a little our satisfaction with the idea of retaliation. Let me repeat that X do not object to retaliation -not at all ; I quite approve of it; but I do not like retaliation which costs us half a million of dollars a year in taxation on an article the taxation on which almost more than the taxation of any other article lays the burden chiefly upon the people least able to bear it. A tax on sugar is essentially a tax on the poor. A family of moderate income will use probably, about as much sugar in the year as will the family of a millionaire. This means that the family of small income will pay more towards the national revenue in proportion to their ability to pay than will the family of the millionaire. The same is true of the taxes on all articles which enter into general consumption. A tax on sugar when it goes beyond a reasonable point is essentially objectionable from the point of view of the agricultural and of the general population of the country, not excluding those who are employed in manufacturing industries.
I take the liberty of saying that if it was desirable to retaliate against Germany- and I agree that under the circumstances it was desirable-I do not think it was desirable to retaliate by hitting ourselves to the amount of half a million dollars a year. It seems to me that if the cost of our sugar is likely to be increased by the amount of half a million dollars a year by the retaliatory duty against Germany, it would have been fair and right to follow the example that was instituted in the case of the preferential tariff, and to have reduced the general tax on sugar so as to even up to consumers generally the increased cost that results from this surtax upon German imports. At this time when we have a swelling revenue and a large surplus, we might very well have a reduction of the duty on sugar rather than an increase, for that is really what the German retaliation amounts to in respect to sugar.
In regard to the proposed duty upon steel rails, I also take issue with the proposition laid own. Of course that duty does not take effect immediately. It may never take effect. Possibly it was never intended to take effect. But if not intended to take effect, it should not appear upon the statute-book, because it commits the House to the principle of protection for protection's sake. Now, if there is one thing that is more necessary than another in the development of this great country of magnificent distances, it is railways, and the great part of their cost, at any rate on the prairies, is the rails, and a duty which increases the cost of rails in this country is to that extent a bar to Mr. OLIVER. -
development. I have read in the papers that we have an estimated consumption of 150,000 tons of steel rails per year, the duty upon which, at $7 per ton, would amount to $1,050,000. That is really a hindrance to the -extent of $1,050,000 to the construction of railways at a time when we are voting from year to year millions of dollars of subsidies to aid in the construction of railways. Now, I am aware that the steel rail industry has its rights the same as any other industry ; but I claim that in this case, as in some other cases that I will mention, the general interest overrides the special interest. I believe that where the interest of this country from one ocean to the other is so largely bound up in railway construction, it is in the general interest that the steel rail industry should be sacrificed for the general interest of the country. I do not know any way yet to give everybody everything that they want, and it is not possible in all cases to do so. We have frequently to give in order to get, in fact, I think that is a rule of life. If we want cheap railways we have to buy rails at the lowest price that the world's market will afford. I would be glad to see the iron industries of Canada developed. At present we are paying considerable bonuses on the production of iron in order to aid in that development. It is, I believe, under the circumstances, a proper policy, a fair policy. For my own part, and speaking as I believe, for the people I represent, we have no objection to that. When we pay bonuses we know how much we are paying, what we are paying them for, and what we are getting for what we are paying. But in the case of a duty we do not know how much we are paying, and we do not know what we are getting for what we are paying. There is all the difference in the world between the two cases. Now, I think that in having bonused the iron industry to the extent that it has been bonused, we have gone quite far enough in that direction. One of the greatest reasons for the revival of manufactures under the present tariff has been that the protective duties on raw Iron which prevailed up to 189G have been reduced or abolished. Now I think it is universally admitted that these iron duties practically strangled Canadian manufactures which used iron. I would be sorry to see that policy reverted to in any degree, and particularly I would be sorry to see it reverted to in the case of such an actual necessity as steel rails.
I believe in giving all industries such incidental protection as a fair revenue tariff will afford them. I have no objection to the protection which is afforded to many of these industries, but there is one which belongs to the class of universal necessities, and which means a special tax on the poorer people and on the industrial classes which, under the tariff as it stands to-day, is anything but a revenue tariff. It stands there

absolutely as a protective tariff quite as mucli as the duty on steel rails-I allude to the duty on coal oil. That duty at the present time fs 5 cents per gallon, which I think amounts to about 75 per cent protection. I claim that is absolutely an unreasonable duty. No industry in this country has a right to such a measure of protection. I would be willing to concede to the coal oil industry a fair measure of protection, a 2c. per gallon duty, if you like ; although I consider that in the case of an article which enters so generally into consumption as coal oil, it should be under an absolutely minimum tariff instead of under a maximum. At a duty of 5 cents per gallon we are paying $50,000 in duty on every million gallons of oil that we import. I presume I am safe in saying that we are paying just as much in the extra price on every million gallons of oil produced in Canada. So that the trade returns do not show the amount of taxation that we are paying on coal oil, by any means. Admitting that 2 cents a gallon of a specific duty on coal oil would be a fair revenue tariff, the difference between what we are paying and what we would be paying under a revenue tariff, amounts to about $30,000 a year on every million gallons of oil consumed in this country. I say that is too much, it is not reasonable. It does not come under the lines of a revenue tariff, it is a burden laid especially upon the agricultural classes of this country, and it is one that I for my part shall vote against on every opportunity that I get.
I will take the liberty of alluding to another protective measure that has been accorded under the present tariff, a protection which can be justified on the grounds I have already mentioned. It was of special advantage to the agricultural industry that binder twine, barbed wire and cream separators were placed upon the free list. That is a measure of protection, I admit, to the agricultural industry. It is justifiable on the ground that that which is the farmer's raw material, a necessity of his occupation and calling, which enters so largely into his every day work, should be subjected to the least possible tax. It is only natural and right that the duties upon such articles should be reduced -to the lowest possible point. In the case of binder twine and barbed wire, industries representing rather raw material than labour, in which the value of the material which goes into their production is so much greater than the amount of labour, the actual labour of the country is not seriously injured by the duty being taken off, it was an eminently proper thing that these articles should be made free of duty. The removal of the duties on these articles has been of special advantage to the agricultural classes, an advantage which they appreciate and one in which in all fairness they are entitled to, because, on many of the articles which they have to buy,* for which they are the principal customers, they are paying, even yet, under this present tariff, the maximum duty of 35 per cent. If -the farmer lias to pay 35 per cent on what he has to buy, when, he lias only a protection of 20 per cent tariff on what he has to sell, it is only fair that he should have these great and recurring necessities absolutely free of duty.
I have said that there were points in the tariff propositions of the hon. Minister of Finance to which I took exception and to which I think the agricultural interests at any rate do take exception. They take exception to the increase in the duties on sugar, to the excessive duty on coal oil and to the proposed duty on steel rails. Now, there is only one way to make the dissatisfaction of a member against the government feit and that is by voting against the government ; and if it were possible on this present occasion to 'express my disapprobation of those points of the policy of the government by my vote on the resolutions before the House I would have great pleasure -no, I would not have great pleasure, but I would feel that I was under the necessity of casting my vote in that way. But, unfortunately, this is not the case. We are here confronted with the proposition of the hon. Minister of Finance to consider his budget as brought down and with the appeal of the hon. leader of the opposition to support his amendment. The amendment offers no satisfactory alternative. Rather, if there is anything contained in the budget proposition of the hon. Minister of Finance which is objectionable to the agricultural interests, that objection is intensified tenfold by the amendment proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition. In the remarks that have been made from the other side of the House one note has run through them all and that is that the agricultural and other duties are not high enough. The * protection on steel rails is not high enough, the retaliation against Germany was-not begun soon enough. There is apparently a sentiment behind the amendment that even the demands of the Manufacturers' Association are not too much to be conceded. It will not answer for our hon. friends on the other side of the House to sneer at us who support the government, to some extent, under protest. It will not do for them to say to us : Vote with us because the government does not do as you wish, for if we voted with them we would be travelling much farther afield from the position which we desire to see maintained. They say :	' The government is a protectionist government, and has chastised you of the agricultural classes with whips ; put us in power and we will chastise you with scorpions.'
We are in a somewhat unfortunate position in that we cannot approve in all particulars of the proposition of the government and at the same time we cannot approve in any particular of the proposals of the op-

1S21
position. There is, it seems to me, something lacking in both the propositions of tlie lion. Minister of Finance and of the hon. leader of the opposition. There is a new condition of affairs arising in this country in finance, in transportation, in commerce, and in manufactures, a condition which is not recognized, of which no note has been taken by either one or the other. I allude to the rise of combines in every line of life. There was a time when we thought that the abolition of duties would prevent the formation of combines. Unfortunately, that is not the fact. On the other hand we are fully of the opinion that the levying of an improper duty certainly tends to the formation of combines. I believe that what this country wants in the way of xiro-tection is protection against combines-combines of capital, combines of industry, combines of transportation, and the policy which is brought forward and which will deal successfully; with these combines is the policy which this country needs and which tbi's country calls for. It is not sufficient simply not to recognize that this condition of affairs exists. It is not sufficient that it did not exist ten years ago or twenty years ago; the fact is that it exists to-day and we are feeling the effects of it. To-day, as was said before, in the North-west Territories, we are paying $9 per thousand more for lumber than we were paying fourteen months ago! as a result of the existence of a combine in lumber. That means $9,000 on each million feet of dressed lumber used in that country. It means an exorbitant tax upon the new settlers in the country, it means a check to immigration, it means a check to prosperity, it means that this government is in duty bound to take measures to "break up that combine, and to bring things to their natural condition. The combines are not confined to lumber. A year ago the paper trade combine was tried in.court and convicted and a reduction in the duty on paper followed. But that is not a sufficient remedy. The evil still exists. I am not able to say what the remedy is, but I say that a remedy Is necessary against these combines in the interest of the people. The first step towards helping combines is a high tariff, and the first step towards breaking them up is a low tariff, or the removal of the duty altogether where a combine is proven to exist.
I wish to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, in reference to the British preference. I have noticed that this preference is an object of serious attack from the other side of the House on nearly all cccasio'ns. Although sometimes it is covert, yet it is continuously made. I regretted very much to hear from the Finance Minister that there was a possibility if not even a probability, that the British preference would be abolished or reduced. Since tlie budget speech was made circumstances have altered so that the conditions which then existed do not exist Mr. OLIVER.
now. The duties on grain imported into Britain have been abolished, and we have not now the same claim upon preferential treatment in their market a's we had a few days ago. But I am not looking at the British preference from the standpoint of retaliation on Britain, or from the British standpoint at all. I am looking at it strictly from the standpoint of a Canadian consumer. I find that the most important imports from Great Britain are cottons and woollens, which are the wear of the masses of the people ; and that which increases the cost of cotton and woollens to the masses of the people is an injury to the people ; that which cheapens the cost of these articles is a benefit to the people. We imported last year $7,000,000 worth of cottons and $10,000,000 worth of woollens from Great Britain. Taking the average duties at 25 per cent, and that is rather below the mark, we find that the saving to the Canadian consumer by the preference on the goods actually imported from Great Britain, amounts to $580,000 on cottons, and $S30.000 on woollens, or a total of $1,410,000 by reason of the British preference on these goods actually imported in one year. I say, Sir, that this is an advantage to the Canadian consumer which no government can afford to ignore. We cannot afford to tax our industrial classes to the extent that is demanded by the cotton and woollen manufacturers of Canada. We are benefiting nine-tenths of the people by the reduced duty on cottons and woollens imported from Great Britain, and if you like to put it in that way, we are injuring the cotton and woollen manufacturers in Canada. But what do these industries amount to. The last census shows that there were 4,000 woollen mill operatives and 0,000 cotton mill operatives in Canada. We are not interested so much in the capital invested in these mills, as we are interested in the operatives in these mills. Put the case in its worst light, and say if you wish that the continuation of the British preference will shut up every cotton and woollen mill in Canada, and even then I will say that Canada cannot afford to carry on the mills at the price demanded by the cotton and woollen manufacturers. But, Sir, this price which they demand is not founded on fact. The truth is that the cotton mills of Canada were never as prosperous as they are to-day, and never were turning out as much goods as they do to-day. As a matter of fact the mills at Valleyfield have doubled their capacity since this government came into power and the British preference was put in force. The cotton industry is one of the strongest evidences of the advantage resulting to manufacturers by reason of the increase in the general prosperity of the country. They have been hardest hit by the lowering of the tariff under the British preference. and still they have achieved that measure of prosperity.

In considering the demands made by these special interests, I would desire to impress upon the government now and henceforth that there are national interests, that there are universal interests to be considered which are entirely paramount to these special interests of the manufacturing concerns. We do not grudge the manufacturing industries all the protection that is coming to them under a fair revenue tariff. They are more than heartily welcome to it ; we wish them all prosperity, hut when they are singled out for special protection and advantage ; when they are put in a position whereby they are to be protected from the stress of commercial depression, while every one else must in the nature of things suffer that to its extreme degree, then it is something that we cannot agree to and that we cannot support any government in agreeing to. It may be possible that on account of the widespread territory covered by agriculture, by the lumbering, by the mining and by the fishing interests, that it is impossible to secure that concentration of pressure which we see exercised in the case of the manufacturing industries. But it will be well for the government to remember that it is there, and that so long as right is right, so long the public interest should be maintained against the demand of any special interest no matter how strongly that demand may he worded or how strongly it is backed up by pressure. It should be remembered that the manufacturing industry has the ear of the press of the country. The manufacturers are in a position to make their voice heard all over the country as the voice of the farmers cannot be heard. They are organized, as the farmers and fishermen are not, but it will be a mistake for this Liberal government to forget the principles upon which they have obtained power and upon which they have been supported in power by yielding in any degree to the demands made upon them by special industries for special protection. If Liberalism means anything, it means that general interests shall prevail against special interests ; it means the masses against the classes, and we look to the present government to maintain Liberalism in this sense.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the House is loosing interest in the budget debate. When Mr. Blain spoke this afternoon I counted just fifteen members on the government side of the House, and when Mr. Oliver rose to speak there were only sixteen. It seems to me that all interest is being lost in the debate, .and that an adjournment would perhaps be in order. However, I understand there are a number of gentlemen who wish to speak and I would like to say a few words myself on the question. It is quite possible that I may not throw much light upon the subject. and that I will have to differ from the hon. members who have spoken before me.
However, they cannot blame me if I do not thoroughly agree with them.
In the first place, I must congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance on his excellent showing in his budget speech. I am sure every man in Canada will be pleased that the government though not instrumental in bringing about the present prosperity, have been at the head of affairs while the country has been progressing so favourably. His showing is certainly a much better one than that of last year. Last year several millions of dollars were added to the national debt, while this year it seems that about 813,000,000 will go to pay off the national debt. Now, Sir, I wish to say a few words from a non-partisan point of view, neither Grit nor Tory, neither Liberal nor Conservative, but from an independent farmer's standpoint. We will try to hew to the line, let the chips fall where they may. I have always held the opinion that trade between all nations and all classes of people should be as free as possible, and with as little restriction as possible. Nearly all nations resort to the system of tariff, or duties on goods to raise the revenue required to support the government and to meet the expenditure of the country. Adequate protection we have had pretty well defined by nearly every hon. gentleman who has spoken. I understand it to mean a higher protective duty than we have at the present time, and that all classes and conditions of the people of Canada are to have a share of protection measured otit to them. Now, Sir, I am at a loss to know how my hon. friend the mover of that amendment is going to protect the farmer. That is what I am here to learn. A high protective duty on such commodities as the people require, gives a few individuals an opportunity to tax the community without giving anything in return either to the government or to help the consumer. For many years past [DOT] Hansard ' has been loaded down with this question. We have heard the same ideas and about the same language that has been used iu this debate, and the country has profited but little from the discussion. Meu invest their capital to manufacture such things as the people want, and then expect the government to allow them to tax the people at their sweet will.
While the lamp holds out to burn.

The hon. gentleman will have an opportunity ; lie is aching for it. For one, I do not object to the government giving a measure of protection when we have the facilities for the production of the raw material in our country ; and when our friends and neighbours are anxious to work that raw material into manufactured goods, I think they should have an opportunity to try to produce the things we require. Therefore I think the



government would be justified in lending assistance to our infant industries.
What particular industry is infant ?	v
You will have an opportunity, my friend.
I know, but I would like to have your idea as to what industry is infantile ?
We want to put them well upon their feet, but after they are well upon their feet, they ought to be able to stand alone.
Is eighteen years long enough ?

That chap is not very well ; you had better give him a job down cellar. The farmers and the working people are willing to pay their fair share of the taxation of this country, but they are not anxious to make millionaires of a few at the expense of all the rest. Canadian manufacturers are able to take care of themselves, and I think I can show you that by bringing in the best evidence we have in this country. ' Industrial Canada,' in its April number says :
Slowly but surely, a Canadian export trade is being built up. Though confronted by many obstacles, the men who are establishing a demand for Canadian goods in foreign markets are gradually making headway amongst the competition of the world. Steamship lines are being acquired by Canadians. Other lines are being subsidized by the Dominion government. Agents are prospecting In distant lands, and manufacturers at home are directing their attention towards foreign conquests	
Many of our firms to-day are self-satisfied. Recent years have been so prosperous that the majority of our manufacturers have been kept
busy with Canadian orders	
We believe that a number of Canadian firms do not even take the trouble to answer inquiries from the foreign field. One instance which has recently come under our notice is that of a large firm in Birmingham whose representative was about to visit Canada, and previous to his departure addressed an inquiry to more than thirty Canadian firms asking them to address him at Toronto, advising him whether they were prepared to undertake export trade and to what extent. To these thirty inquiries only eight answers were received, the firms favoured with the opportunity not having shown even the courtesy of a reply. Such an attitude injures the whole prospect of Canadian trade and our firms would do well, even if they cannot undertake the execution of orders at the present time, to look ahead and retain always the confidence of foreign buyers.
That proves most conclusively that the manufacturers of all classes of goods have no reason to complain. It is useless to attempt to build up industries without natural advantages. We have the raw materials, we must have coal and electric power or water power, otherwise we cannot compete successfully in manufacturingI Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
with other nations who have these advantages. But if we have these advantages and cheap food and money, our Canadian industries should be able to hold their own, even if not protected against foreign producers. Our farmers and other classes of Canada are willing to assist our manufacturers, but are not willing to pamper and pet them for ever. We are referred to the high protective system of the United States, and I might say that one half of the discussion on the present budget has been taken up with what has occurred in the United States. It seems to me that we have enough to do at home and would do better to confine our own attention to our own business and leave the United States alone. But since the United States are pointed to as an argument in favour of protection let me point out that the protective system in that country has been the means of making many millionaires and some multi-millionaires, but has not made the average people of that country any better off than the same people in other countries. It has certainly not done anything for the farmers because they are poor men. In Canada we do not want any tyrants, we do not want any one-man power, but we want wealth distributed fairly among all classes and conditions of men. A very large minority of the American people are opposed to a high protective tariff, and were it not for the fact that the United States enjoy free trade among fifty commonwealths, comprising 84,000,000 people, their system of high protection would have exploded long ago. The manufacturers of the United States and Canada are selling their goods cheaper abroad than to their own people. Take the manufacturers of machinery, in which every farmer is interested. Some time ago a number of binders were smashed up in a railway accident, and the manufacturers sued the railway company for damages. During the hearing, the evidence showed that the cost price of these binders was less than $40, and yet the retail price to the farmers was $110. If our manufacturers are making such immense profits, I do not think it reasonable for our government to entertain any proposition to raise the duties. When discussing this question with a friend of mine some time ago, I told him that every machine I had on my farm was made in Canada, I said that there was sufficient loyalty about me to buy everything in Canada. Well, he replied, I do not see where the loyalty comes in. Had you bought that machine in the United States, you would have had to pay $20 into the revenue of this country. Which is the most loyal-the man who pays $20 to the government, or the man who pays $20 to the manufacturers ? I leave that nut for my hon. friends around me to crack. We sometimes lay the flattering unction to our souls that we are very loyal, but when we hear the other side we begin to doubt whether our patriotism will stand washing.

We have heard considerable about this German treaty, and I felt rather pleased when the hon. Minister of Finance told us that he was about to retaliate on these people who had tried to injure us by refusing to give us the benefit of the favoured-nation clause. But when I come to think the whole matter over, it begins to dawn on me that I might be in the position in which I used to be when younger. I have read a good deal of Scripture and have tried to live up to it. One Scriptural advice is that when struck on the right cheek, we should turn the left. I have lived up to that as much as I could, but whenever I turned my left cheek and was struck on that, then my hand was ready to strike the aggressor down if possible. That is just the way I felt about this German treaty. But when we begin to question whether there is not tco much muscular force on the other side and that we might suffer in consequence, another aspect of the case presents itself. We have to think before we act. However, whether we have sufficient muscular force or not, it is worth our while to test it and teach the nations of the world that Canada dare say her soul is her own.
Another strong point made by the hon. Finance Minister was concerning the question of preferential trade. We held the whip hand over those Britishers, and if they would not give us preferential trade in grain we might at some time consider the advisability of abrogating the preferential clause in our tariff. What about us poor Canadians ? Ain't we in it ? I think we are. Take the case of a widow with a family of little children. She has to clothe them-that is as necessary in this country as feeding them. She goes to a merchant tailor for a suit for her five year old boy. The merchant understands the case. He shows two suits, both the same price, $5, and both fitting for the boy's wear. Here, says the merchant, is one suit, which was made in England. Here is another, at the same price, but it may not be quite so good a class of cloth. If you buy the English suit, you pay a dollar into the Dominion treasury-if you buy the other one, you pay the dollar just the same, but it goes into the manufacturer's pocket. There is patriotism again. The poor widow says : Surely, I don't have to pay a dollar into either. But the clothier answers: Madam, remember that if we had not the preferential trade that Mr. Fielding gave us, you would have to pay sixty cents more. Then it begins to dawn upon her that preferential trade is a good thing for her as a Canadian. I am not sure that I have made the case clear to some of the obtuse-minded gentlemen I see about me. Some fifteen years ago, I was in North Britain. I do not care to tell all the little incidents that have happened in my life; some of them might be against me. I was in Glasgow, and as my business was 58i
done for the day, I went with a friend to the extensive Coatbridge iron works. Every one who knows anything about that section knows of this great industry. It was wonderful to go through the works at night with the furnaces in full blast. The foreman was very kind-a canny Scot. He learned that I came from Canada, and that may have made him all the more courteous to me. Since that time, we have had the King's coronation, and more Canadians have been seen in Great Britain of late. But, at that time we were quite a novelty. The foreman said: You come from Canada ? What business brought you over? I told him that I had come with some cattle. Have you sold them ? Yes, sold them on Glasgow market. He said ; I was reading in the papers this morning that the Canadian government has raised the duty on bar iron-the stuff that they were rolling out there in immense quantities-to ?13 per ton. I said I was sorry for that, and if I had been in the Canadian parliament I would not have voted for that. That made him think I was somebody of importance, I suppose. He said : Now, my friend, you brought some cattle from Canada ; did you have to pay any duty to bring them here ? No, sir. You don't know how badly I felt to think that we placed a duty on the product on their industry, while they allowed my finished product to go into their country free. I told him I would do all I could to remedy that when I got back-and I have been a long time trying to do it. I would commend this illustration to those who are harping on the idea that Great Britain does not give us a preference. Why is she not giving us a preference all the time ? Has she a duty on anything coming from Canada except tobacco-and we don't have much of that to sell-and whisky ? It is true, they have the embargo on the cattle, but I believe that will be removed when we can show a clean bill of health.
Another thing that we have heard for the last twelve months is ' Canada for the Canadians.' It sounds splendid at first-ypu would think everybody would throw up his liat and hurrah for it. But when you examine it and think the matter over, you will find, as in fihe other case, there is nothing in it. Suppose that the British people who are our best customers, were to say that as we are crying Canada for Johnny Can-nuck, so they would cry Britain for John Bull, and were to turn their deer parks and pheasant preserves into grazing lands and raise their own stock. I tell you, to-morrow we would be begging those people to take our stock. What would be the value of our lands if we had not a market there for our cheese, beef, apples and all our surplus products ? It is our duty as Canadians to try to keep that British market open, and to see that no foe shuts us out from it. That is where we get our income from. That is

the goose that lays the golden egg, and we must see to it that she is not killed. Do you think that when you sell your stock or your cheese to Great Britain, they are going to pay you gold. You need not expect it; Great Britain will not send gold either in bullion or in dust. She wants to sell you her products, and, if she cannot do it, she will buy stuff from the nations that will buy from her. You are handicapped if you do not trade with the nations that trade with you, because the law of trade is not goods for gold but goods for goods. It is our duty to trade with our best customers. Our country is progressing by leaps and bounds, and the government must move with it. It is the duty of the government to use every means in its power to help all those who are trying to help themselves. And they say that the best way to do that is to leave the farmers alone and not put a duty on what they need to buy and reduce their purchasing power. By helping the farmers you are helping every other class. So, be very careful what you, do. Explore and exploit all our new domain where there is iron, pulpwood, nickel or anything else. Lend a helping hand to those who are willing to put money into these things. But do not pamper them for ever. Help them at the start, and they will soon be able to help themselves.
Now with regard to this steel rail question I feel somewhat like my bon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver). These railway companies that are asking for subsidies from this government will need to double their request if you put a duty on steel rails. They will have to pay 87 a ton more duty. For myself, I am opposed to giving subsidies to railways. I believe the time has come when capitalists have got sufficient money to build their own railways. If we give them money, we should see that we have security, we should take first mortgage on the road, and have a voice in its management, and make it carry our mails and do our work for the money that we grant it. Now, Sir, it is a question to my mind, when we give them $7 duty and $6 in bounty, whether $13 a ton would not be too much to give for the purpose of starting a steel rail industry. However, if it is decided by the wisest men in this country that that would be the best plan, I am not going to object; let us try it for a while.
The next point I will touch upou is the question of binder twine, in which all the farmers are interested. That also is their raw material. It takes 45 cents worth of binder twine to bind an acre of good wheat, so that on every acre we have to spend 45 cents, whether we get anything back or not. Now it is the manufacturers of binder twine who are asking for protection, I understand. I was pleased when the duty was taken off binder twine, because I believed that our Canadian manufacturers were able to compete with the United States manufacturers.

But if it is true, as has been stated, that the Americans get a rebate on their raw material, that there is a monopoly of manilla in that country, and that our people cannot get the sisal used in the manufacture of binder twine, then it will be a matter for consideration as to whether we should give them a duty or not. But, if we do, we must see that the duty is not so high as to prevent the Americans selling our farmers twine so that our manufacturers may not have a monopoly. The binder twine people are no better than others, and they will form a combination if they are able, and make the farmers pay higher prices. I do not believe in bonuses, but there are times, perhaps, when they are necessary. Now, Mr. Speaker. I apologize to the House for having spoken so long, though the apology may not be so much needed, because there are so few here. But those who are absent will be sorry in the morning that they were not here.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. E. VROOMAN (South Victoria, Ontario).
speechtext:
Of all the questions mentioned in the budget speech, perhaps the financial question is the most important to this country. All other questions treated in the budget speech are more or less affected by the financial position. When the revenues of the country are buoyant, when the treasury is overflowing, it gives an impulse to all the departments of the government, and the public machinery moves on easily. I have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that when times are good, people are satisfied, and are disinclined to a change, in fact they like to leave things as they are. There is a disinclination for experiments. I think this government have taken full advantage of these conditions, and have decided to leave things pretty much as they were before. In fact, when we look around and ask ourselves what they have done, we cannot find an answer ; especially are we puzzled to find out what they have done after having made such large expenditures. Perhaps, after all, judging from the little things they have done, it is better that they should have not attempted great things, because if they had, they would probably have injured the country. I was pleased to listen for the third time to the story the Finance Minister had to tell us about prosperity and good times. I was ready to make some allowance for the ring of exultation in his voice when he announced that wonderful surplus, the largest surplus we have ever had in the Dominion of Canada. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I contend that the Conservative surpluses, though not as large, were more creditable to the government under the circumstances in which they were gathered.
I have always thought, Mr. Speaker, that this government was in many respects very fortunate. They came into power contemporaneously with good times. That statement does not need any proof. If we look

up the statistics of those days, we will find plenty of evidence to show that before they came into power good times had begun to revive. We all remember the times of depression from 1892 to 1896. The world over there was financial depression and stagnation. Under those circumstances, we were fortunate in having at the head of our financial affairs a very able man, who succeeded in conducting the ship of state through financial storms, while on the other side of the line, many monetary institutions tottered or went to the wall. In Canada our banks and corporate institutions all weathered the storm, with, I think, only one exception, a little bank up in the city of Winnipeg. But what was the course of the opposition in those days ? The opposition thought it was a good time to make an onslaught on the government, they thought the time had come when they might possibly attain to power. They made various specious promises that I need not detail to this House They threw into the arena of public discussion, a very troublesome religious question, and owing to the discontent thus created, and the prevailing hard times, the Liberal party succeeded in attaining to power. But we have discovered, after looking back over the six years that they have been in power, that the Liberal party made a better opposition than they do a government. I do not say even then, very much for their opposition when they were on this side of the House. During their long occupation of seats on this side of the House they in-culated to perfection the science of criticism and of faultfinding. They arrived at a perfection in that regard that we on this side of the House do not hope to emulate. But since they have been occupying the treasury benches, we have not discovered in them any evidence of constructive statesmanship. Now, while the Liberal party were in opposition, and especially during those hard times, they were wonderfully alarmed about the financial condition of the country, and in a resolution adopted at the Liberal convention in 1893, in this city, they expressed their alarm in this way. Mr. Speaker, you will indulge me if I recall a little ancient history. Perhaps the House has never heard of this resolution before :
We cannot but view with alarm the large increase of the public debt and of the controllable annual expenditure of the Dominion, and the consequent undue taxation of the people under the governments that have been continuously in power since 1878 ; and we demand strict economy in the administration of the government of the country.
They really deserve our pity when we consider that during all these long years they lived in this constant state of alarm. As a practical professional man, I understand the wearing nature of that condition of the nervous svstem, that constant state of alarm. From 1S93 to 1896 we had that party constantly affirming that position, and
I will draw from ancient history the expressions of some of these lion, gentlemen. The present hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said :
I say that it is a disgrace and a shame to the government that have been entrusted with our affairs that they come down to us and ask for an expenditure of $38,300,000 a year for federal purposes. Sir, the thing is utterly unjustifiable.
The present Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock) said in 1895 :
There is nothing to warrant this enormous expenditure of nearly $38,000,000 except the fact that we are burdened down with debt and with office-holders, great and small.
I have not heard that these office holders have been dismissed, or if they have been dismissed, deserving followers have been put in their places. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said :
The Liberal party, if in power, could at once reduce the public expenditure and effect other savings to the. extent of five million dollars per annum, without impairing the efficiency of the service.
The right hon. the present leader of the House (Et. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said :
If we get into power we will follow the example of Mr. Mackenzie ; and I say that, although we may not be able to bring the expenditures to what they were under him, we can reduce the amount two, yes, three millions of dollars per year.
Well, they came into power and in six vears we find an annual expenditure of $64,000,000 which is just $20,000,000 more than the expenditure when they came into power. We find that in the last six years of their rule they spent $101,417,000 more than was spent during the last six years of Conservative rule. This is an immense amount of money. We have been told that there have been great public works undertaken in this country. The hon. Minister of Finance said the other day that they had provided liberally for public works. I have been trying to think what has been done in this country with this large expenditure what great public works have they built, and I am not able to settle on anything of importance that has been done. They have a public debt of $271,000,000 as against a debt of $258,000,000 when they came into office. They levied taxes last year to the amount of $43,389,000, whereas, when they came into office they found taxation to the amount of $27,759,000. During six years of rule by these hon. gentlemen we do not find that they have manifested any particular alarm. The alarm subsided when these gentlemen achieved power and we now find that they have passed into a state of quiescence and rest. We do not hear any expressions from these hon. gentlemen now about the unjustifiable expenditure of the government; in fact, I sometimes think that members of the opposition are very lax in I applying the proper epithets to that kind of

thing. I do not wish to burden the House with statistics, because, in this debate, we have had a good many statistics. But, I would like for my own purpose to refer to the taxation imposed upon the people of the country. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), gave us the particulars of the taxation for the last six years of the administration of lion, gentlemen opposite and for the last six years of the administration of the previous government and he was answered in that regard by the kon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. If kon. gentlemen will look at the record of taxation from 1891 to 1896 they will find that taxation was not increased but that it was actually decreased. During the period from 1891 to 1896 there was a falling off in taxation, but from 1896 to 1902 we find taxation rapidly increasing. The present government found the taxation at $27,759,000 when they came into office, while in the last report, we find that the taxation imposed upon the people has been increased to $43,000,000. In the last six years the government have taken out of the people in taxation $44,000,000 more than the taxation imposed upon the people during the previous six years. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce undertook to explain that away and this is the way that he did it. He said :
That is the hon. leader of the opposition-*
Has paid no attention whatever to the difference between the real taxation inflicted on the people under a protective tariff, and the actual taxation inflicted on the people under a revenue tariff, even if it be a high one.
I have tried to understand what a revenue tariff was and what a protective tariff was, but I have never been right in my conclusion if the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce is an authority upon the subject. We have the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) saying this in his speech :
The tariff of this country is practically the same that was adopted in 1897.
Now the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce further said :
The difference is this, that substantially the great bulk of the taxes go into the treasury under the present tariff, whereas under the administration which preceded ours an enormous percentage of the taxes which the people of Canada had to pay did not go into the treasury but went to swell the profits of private individuals. The people.under our tariff have the satisfaction at any rate of knowing that what is taken out of them goes into the treasury, and can be used for the benefit of the whole people.
The hon. ex-Minister of Public Works said :
The revision of the tariff of 1897 has placed it about 2 per cent less high than it was before. We did not do more than that ; and when iny hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was this afternoon denouncing the former tariff, the tariff that I supported my-Mr. VROOMAN.
self, when he was telling us that the tariff enacted in 1879 and kept on the statute-book up to 1897 had simply allowed the manufacturers to pocket the money of the people, I was saying to myself, if it was so, I do not know what it is now, because there is not much difference in the two tariffs ; the present tariff is about the same thing. We even raised the tariff in 1897 as against the United States on many articles.
It seemed to me when I heard that sort of argument coming from the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce that it was a very fallacious argument. I could noti help but believe that the hon ex-Minister of Public Works was right in this matter and that, as is practically admitted by the government supporters, the tariff is the same as that which has been in force since 1879 with some few slight exceptions and the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works says that the government even raised the tariff against the United States in some particulars. What is the principal reason why taxation fell off in the last six years of Conservative rule ? Here is what the ex-Minister of f'inace (Mr. Foster) said in 1891 :
In 1891 we remitted taxation on sugar-it came into effect the latter part of that year- to the extent of $227,477, and we had a surplus of $155,977. In 1892, the remission of sugar taxation, calculated on an equal consumption, was $5,200,000, and still we had a surplus of $1,354,555. In 1893, calculated on the consumption, the remission of taxation on raw sugar and other sugar amounted to $4,000,000, and we had a deficit of $1,210,232. In 1894, the remission of sugar taxation was $4,821,000, and we had a deficit of $4,153,875. And in 1895, after which we placed again the duty on raw sugar, the remission of total taxation was $5,603,521, and the deficit had come down to $330,551. What is the summing of the matter ? It is that in that period there was taxation remitted to the tune of $19,800,000, but there was a net deficit of $4,184,227. So that consequently there was given back to the country, in the remission of taxation, over and above the deficit which had to be provided out of capital, the sum of $15,000,000.
That is the reason there was no increase in the taxation. But with all the large surpluses that this government has had we do not find that they remit any taxes to the people. On the contrary, they continue to take money out of the pockets of the people, and to take all that they decently can. Bast year the expenditure for all purposes was $63,970,000 against an expenditure of $44,000,000 in 1896, when the Conservatives were in power, or an increase of $19,874,000 under Liberal rule, and on the top of all that the national debt has been increased as well. It was unfair for the Finance Minister to compare eighteen years of Conservative rule as to expenditure with the six years of Liberal rule, because we all know that during the eighteen years the Conservatives were in power vast public works were undertaken and completed. I shall take the liberty of reading from the ' Monetary Times ' an article on the budget speech of last year, which applies equally

well to the conditions that prevail this year, and I assume that the ' Monetary Times ' is not a party paper. It says :
The Finance Minister has been most fortunate in taking up his story at the beginning ot a cycle of prosperity and expansion, which succeeded the world-wide depression of the previous five years, and drew to its close in 1895 ; and in having had five full and growing years for succeeding recitals. We may also say that he was fortunate in having had as his predecessors in the government, men who spent largely and builded wisely in preparing the ground, without which no such results as called forth his and our congratulations could have been possible.
The budget speech shows an almost dizzying progress to have been made in other respects than in trade, and throws into bold relief the striking change in faith and practice since 1896. Never in the history of Canada were such vast figures dealt with by a Finance Minister in point of revenue and expenditure. Receipts from taxes $38,743,000 in 1901, compared with $37,759,285 in 1896. Total revenues, -which of course all come out of the people's pockets, $52,500,000, as against $36,600,000. Total expenditure $57,900,000, compared -with $41,700,000, and a net public debt of $268,000,000, as compared with $258,000,000-mark the change in five years. For 1902 it is stated that the total to be gathered for the treasury will be $57,000,000, the total expenditure $65,000,000, and the addition to the debt will be $6,000,000.
This fairly takes away one's breath, the sums are so vast, and the increase so rapid. Yet it is not recorded that Sir Richard Cartwright either swooned or swore, or that any of the old advocates of economy and reduction did else than cheer the minister as he placidly made these announcements on the authority and with the sanction of a Liberal government. _ And yet, apart from the change of front indicated in the parts', these figures challenge the serion i attention of every thoughtful citizen. Granted that the country is prosperous, is it wise to set so rapid a pace, and raise to such a height the scale of expenditure, which once raised it will be found almost impossible to lower ? It is well to remember that as the prices of staples rise-and there have been marked advances in price in many lines of recent years-the amount recived from customs taxation rises, for it is largely ad valorem. Then, when prices fall, the amount of customs revenue falls. In prosperous times, with a buoyant revenue, is it prudent to spend it all and add so many millions besides to a debt already too large ? For $13 per head or $65 per family for one year's government is a tremendous charge. Giving all due force to the contention that we are a growing country, and must needs provide generously for the public service, this headlong rush torward in taxation and expenditure, seemingly unchecked by bit or bridle, invites reflection on the part of business men and thoughtful citizens. These piping times will not always continue, and the overdrain of to-day hastens the exhaustion of tomorrow. We cry a warning and a halt before the rush has become a rout in which moderation and prudence lose iheir meaning and their force. A! this rate wre know not where we shall end, for, though '.he minister hints at limits to the tide of prosperity, he apparently sets none to the volume of expenditure.
That article from this respectable journal speaks better than I can of the present
financial condition of the country. We are well aware that in a new country like this, expenditure must increase and the people of Canada are perfectly willing to meet that increased expenditure, but there is a limit to everything. When our expenditure increases by leaps and bounds as it has done in the past few years, we naturally want to know what it is expended for, and when we come to inquire into the details we find that there is a wholesale waste of public money. Take the expenditure for the census as an example. We have had four censuses since confederation. The census of 1871 cost $511,000; the census of 1881, $552,000 ; the census of 1891, $549,000, an average for each of the three censuses taken by the Conservative government of $540,000. But in 1901, under a Liberal government, the census has cost $1,121,513, up to date. The Minister of Agriculture told us last year that the reason for this was because they asked so many more questions and elicited so much more information from the people. That may be true, for we all remember that the government issued a circular to their enumerators, instructing them that they were to get the ages of all the young men who were about to become twenty-one years old, and likely to support the government, so as to have them ready to put on the voters' list for the coming election. I asked the Minister of Agriculture what was the cost of taking the census in my own constituency, and that is a fair sample of what has occurred everywhere else. The fact of the matter is that they have uselessly spent double the money that the Conservatives did. The Minister of Agriculture told me that the population of my riding in 1891 was 20,455 and in 1901 it was 19,953, or about 500 less. But there were seventeen enumerators in 1891 and 39 enumerators in 1901. In 1891 the expense of taking the census in my riding was $1,253, and in 1901 it was $2,663. The Minister of Agriculture further told us that in 1891 the enumerators were allowed nothing for transportation but in 1901 they received $1.50 a day for horse hire. The cost of taking the census in that small riding in 1901 was just double what it was in 1891, and that increase can easily be explained when we find that every sorehead of the Liberal party and every party heeler in the constituency was appointed as an enumerator at the expense of the country, in order to get him back into the traces before the election. That is an illustration of where the money goes under this Liberal government. The fact is that this government, and to some extent they are justified in it, have not been disturbing the trend of things since they came into power. Times have been good and the revenue bouyant, and they have been allowing things to float along, as it were. But there is one thing which they have been very active about, and that is in looking after the party inter-

1S40
ests and placing their friends In good safe positions. As to the general interest of the country they are doing nothing. As a competent authority for that, I will quote from the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister, delivered at the Toronto Fair banquet on the 27th of August, 1901. He was replying to the toast of the parliament of Canada, and he said :
At the present time the government was in the happy position of having little to do. It had been said, ' Happy the man who has no history,' and it might with equal truth be asserted, ' Happy the nation that has no history.' He was in the peculiar position of a reformer who had nothing to reform. There had been a time when he had wanted to reform everything, but nowadays, added Sir Wilfrid, ' I find that I am very much of a Conservative.'
This, though somewhat of a confession, was part of the common history of mankind ; the young man is ardent for change and thinks the world is out of joint ; but as a man advances in life he feels as do the majority of men in parliament, that this is a good world to live in after all, and things run on very well if they are let alone.
So, Mr. Speaker, I bad just occasion for saying wbat I did about this matter. The sentiments expressed there are quite praiseworthy ; I do not take any exception to them, though I doubt very much about his being a Conservative, and have they been lived up to ?
Now, looking at the Trade and Navigation Returns, we see that our total imports for home consumption last year amounted to $202,701,595, and our total exports to $211,640,280, which I take to include coin and bullion. As we analyse these figures, keeping in mind the preferential features of the tariff, they are somewhat interesting. We find that we imported from Great Britain $49,206,062 and from the United States $120,814,750. The lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) says these large imports from the United States are due to geography. I am ready to admit that geography has a good deal to do with them. We import a great deal from the United States that we would not perhaps import if the two countries were not in such close proximity ; hut that fact does not account for the whole difference. We have this broad fact, that while a preference has been given to English goods in our market, we imported only $49,000,000 from Great Britain, while we imported $120,000,000 from the United States. We get a better idea when we consider the increases. Since 1S98, the increase in the imports from England [DOT]was $16,705,145, while the increase in the imports from the United States was $42.109,160. The history of the British preference must be a source of great humiliation to hon. members on the government side of the House. When that preference was granted to English goods in our market in 1898, we remember with what a blowing of horns and heating of drums it was ushered in. We could not hear the last of it;

we would not hare tliese blockades that we have to-day. When blockades of freight take place I think the government should approach that great corporation and urge them to improve their equipment. Now this transportation question is to a great extent an agricultural question, because it is the agricultural products that have forced this question to the front. These products are increasing, and' the farmers are becoming greatly interested in this question of transportation. But the farmer does not care very much how his goods get to market, whether they go through this route or that, so long as he gets them to market in good season, and gets good returns. A good deal of fault has been found with the Grand Trunk for making its terminus at Portland. We have the ex-Minister of Public Works declaring that there is no patriotism in money or business. He said he did not blame the Grand Trunk for making its terminus at Portland, because Portland was its natural port. The shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway have a right to expect the best possible dividends, and Portland being the natural port, the Grand Trunk carry a large quantity of grain to that port. It is the same with the farmer. He does not care which way his grain gets to the market so long as it gets there by the cheapest and safest route. His chief desire is to get his goods on the market in the best condition.
Another important question I wish to discuss is that of assisting the construction of railways by subsidies. Up to this time there has been an immense sum of money spent on the construction of railways. This country has spent $230,000,000 in money subsidies to railways, besides land grants and freedom from taxation. According to the last Statistical Year-book, we have now 18,140 miles of railway. The Dominion government has contributed toward their construction at the rate of $9,083 per mile; the provincial governments have contributed $1,771 per mile, and the municipalities have contributed $892 per mile. So our railways in Canada have been subsidized at the rate of $11,740 per mile. I think, Mr. Speaker, the day has arrived when this expenditure is becoming unnecessary. We certainly have reached a state of development when railway corporations should build their own roads. But as long as it remains the policy of this government to give subsidies, just so long will private enterprises refuse to put money into them. It seems inconsistent that we should talk about railway subsidies aim freight blockades in the same breath. U ith freight waiting to be carried such as ^ e hear about and we know to be the case surely those ventures ought to pay It ought to be considered a great concession to secure a charter to build a road in this country, and the government ought not to be asked to contribute. What is the history of railway building in the United States ?

The people there have had to meet much the same conditions as those existing in Canada, and it is natural to inquire as to the policy they have pursued in reference to this question. So far as the United States government is concerned, it has never given a single cash bonus; all the aid it has ever given has been confined to assistance to transcontinental lines. The moneys advanced to them were secured by mortgage bonds which, with few exceptions, have been paid off, so that it has received back in interest and principal far more than the original amount advanced. In addition, the United States government has made large grants in public lands. The Western States, though, had a different policy, and gave so largely that several of them became practically bankrupt; but to-day no railway bonuses are given in the United States. In the Eastern States no bonuses in money or land were ever given. At the present time the railways constructed in Canada, with scarcely an exception, have been subsidized by the Dominion government to the extent of $3,200 per mile, but latterly the Dominion subsidy has been increased, so that if a road costs over $15,000 per mile it receives an additional subsidy of 50 per cent of the excess of the cost until the total Dominion subsidy reaches $6,400 per mile. The usual subsidy given by the provinces is $3,000 per mile, and is in addition to the Dominion subsidy.
The difference in the Canadian policy regarding railway construction and the United States policy, is well illustrated in the bridge built at or near the town of Cornwall, Ont. That part of the bridge lying in Canadian territory received subsidies from the Dominion and provincial governments to the extent of $125,000, and is practically free from taxes; while that part lying in American territory received no subsidy and contributes a substantial tax to the State of New York. The New York and Ottawa Railway was bonused on this side of the St. Lawrence, but received no bonus in the United States. Yet over the subsidized line in Ontario the fare is three cents per mile. And over its entire length on the other side the fare is two cents per mile. The passenger rate in New York is two cents per mile, and in the State of Michigan two cents. The Grand Trunk Railway has given a two-cent rate over all its lines in Michigan. If the subsidies that we give to railways had the effect of reducing rates, there might be a good deal to be said for them, for we would then receive back in the form of cheap rates at least a part of the outlay. But unfortunately the subsidies that we pay are not applied to any such purpose. They are realized on at once by those who receive them, and the road which is built is mortgaged and stocked to its limit.
Now, I would like to quote from a speech delivered by Mr. W. D. Gregory to the farm-
