ers of North York, as reported in the ' Farmers Sun ':
Let me quote you some of the rates which prevailed last year between the Western States and the seaboard, and between Ontario points and the seaboard, and the prices -which at the same time the Ontario farmer and the farmer in the United States received. In May last year the Grand Trunk Railway carried grain arriving by lake at the town of Midland, from Midland to Montreal for 4i cents per bushel, including terminal charges. At the same time it charged 8 4-10 cents per bushel for carrying from Midland to Montreal grain raised in the county of Simcoe and loaded on the cars from the local elevators. In October last, the rate on grain from Duluth to Montreal via the Canada Atlantic Railroad was 8J cents per hundredweight, and the rate from Fort William to Montreal via the Midland Railroad 10 cents per hundred-weight.
At the same time the rate from Markdale, Ontario, to Montreal, was 161 cents per hundred-weight, or almost double the rate charged for the carriage of grain from Duluth to Montreal over a road heavily subsidized by you. At the same time the rate from Buffalo to Liverpool via New York was 111 cents per hundredweight, and the rate from Toronto to Liverpool 171 cents per hundred-weight. Is it, therefore, surprising to find that at this time No. 2 red winter wheat was selling at Chicago for 691 cents per bushel, and at Milwaukee from G8 to 69 cents per bushel, while in Western Ontario the price was from 65 cents to 651 cents per bushel, and at Toronto 66 cents per bushel, the latter price being the highest then paid in the province ?
It has often been wondered why wheat sells at a little higher price at Chicago than at Toronto, but the freight rates do the whole thing. It is explained easily in that way :
Another aggravating feature of the situation from the farmers standpoint is the frequent difficulty of securing sufficient cars for the local shipments. We all know the Midland railway ; yet at one time not very long ago local grain buyers had to wait for weeks before getting a car to ship the produce of Ontario, while train load after train load of cars loaded with American grain rolled by the local station on their way to the seaboard. A large portion of this American grain had been accepted by the railroad subject to the condition that it should be delivered at the seaboard at a certain time, and in order that it might be delivered, Canadian shippers were deprived of the cars they might otherwise have received. The scheme of diverting American grain to Canadian routes did not work to your advantage on that occasion.
In my opinion it is not in the interests of the country that we should subsidize railways any more unless for colonization purposes and then there should be a lien taken on the road. I just want to give the answer to a question asked by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) the other day which was given by the hon. Postmaster General. The hon. member for West Elgin asked :
Has the government made any efforts to induce any of the immigrants coming to Canada to settle in Ontario ?
I think the hon. Postmaster General made rather a curt reply to that hon. gentleman, and I do not consider that he gave a proper reply at all. This is the answer that he gave :

The government in promoting immigration into Canada leaves it to the immigrants themselves to select the places in the Dominion where they desire to settle.
These poor immigrants are in the hands of an agent. If the agent were instructed by the hon. Minister of Agriculture as to the necessities of Ontario it would be an easy matter for him to switch off a number of these people and direct them to locate in Ontario. I want to bring this matter to the attention of the hon. acting Minister of Agriculture, because the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) is not here.
I regret he is not. I hope he may be at work where he is for the advantage of Canada. I understand he is cultivating very friendly relations with the Japanese. I am told that he is rapidly assuming the manner and even the appearance of these people and that he would be very easily mistaken for one of that nationality now. I hope the government will not risk losing permanently the services of that valuable minister. We have been spending half a million of dollars on immigration agents abroad, and we have coming into this country to-day an immense number of immigrants. It seems like the irony of fate that the government hardly know what to do with the immigrants now coming into this country when only a few years ago these hon. gentlemen were declaring that the Canadian Pacific Railway would not pay for the axle grease. I think under the circumstances that the money spent ou agents in Europe might be brought home and used in providing accommodation for these immigrants here. I believe that the tide of immigration which has set in will continue and that the expenditure in foreign fields may be reduced, or that it may be brought to this country and used in looking after the comfort of these immigrants. I do not know that I would advocate the reduction of the expenditure, but there is no occasion for increasing it. The hon. Minister of Agriculture must know that this is an important question in the province of Ontario. It is becoming a matter of concern to the farmers in that province. The tenant farmers and labourers have gone to the west and a farmer cannot rent his farm, he cannot sell it and he cannot work it for want of labour. I have heard farmers in the province of Ontario make that statement again and again. They say : Are we to turn our farms into commons and allow the cattle to run over them ! This condition is brought about by the fact that there is no labour to be had in the province of Ontario. I think it would be very easy for the immigration agents . to

divert some of the stream of immigration into the province of Ontario. We have had deputations of farmers from the province waiting upon the local government and asking them to do something. There has been a promise made, hut, owing to fortuitous circumstances, the government at Toronto has not had time to do anything. This is a matter that I desire to impress upon the attention of the government. This is the condition of affairs in the province of Ontario and I want to bring it before the government in the interest of the farming community because I represent a farming constituency and I am a farmer myself. I think I am a practical farmer because I was born on the farm, and in fact, I have lived off the proceeds of the farm all my life.
Now, I want to say something for the benefit of the hon. Postmaster General. I do not want to discuss that vexed question of his surplus at all. It seems clear that the reports are all askew in regard to this matter. They will not agree. The Auditor General's Report says one thing, the Public Accounts say another thing and the Postmaster General's Report, which would be expected to put the most favourable light upon it says another thing. There is one thing that I want to call to the attention of the House and it is the inferior postal service that is given in the province of Ontario. I know men engaged in mail carrying who are not getting as much as they should; yet, the hon. Postmaster General is supposed to look after the wages that labouring men get. There is another point that I want the hon. Postmaster General to take a note of. If this were not going down in ' Hansard ' I might as well be talking to a vacuum, or to vacancy, because

speechtext: Hear, hear.
I hope the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Ross) is enjoying himself. I did not know he so considered himself.
Surely yon would not call ' Hansard ' a vacuum.

In Ontario the question of free mail delivery has become a real live issue. The farmers are asking for the free delivery of mails at their own homes. When you come to investigate this question yon will find that it is a very important one. We know that farm life in Ontario, as elsewhere, is a hard life. I have no doubt there are many farmers who are well to do, who make a considerable amount of money and who have a good time, but the average farmer is not in that position. He works hard and his life Is a monotonous one, so much so, that the boys and the girls leave home. The farmer, when his sons leave home cannot get help and anything that will make farm life more comfortable and enjoyable is going to do a great deal to im-Mr. VROOMAN.
prove the condition of the farmer. What I want to see is the adoption of a system of free mail delivery that will bring the farmer in contact with the outside world every day, so that, the boys insteads- of going down to the village to hear the latest dirty stories and other trash in the evening he will have some inducement to remain al) home. I want every farmer in Ontario who can afford it to have a telephone. That telephone question is coming to the front and I was glad to hear it discussed the other day at the Railway Committee. If the farm home has the telephone in it, if the farm home has the daily paper in it, then, the boys, when they come in from their work will be perfectly willing to stay there and if we can get them these comforts and other modern facilities such as the electric cai-, I am sure hon. gentlemen will agree) with me when I say that the attractiveness of home life on the farm will be much enhanced.
There Is no use arraying class against class as the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Davis) did. We are enjoying prosperity and peace and plenty in Canada to-day, and what we want to do is to make the home happy. This is an agricultural country above all and it is my opinion that the interests of the farmers are kept too much in the back ground. It is true that the tariff is an important question, but the Minister of Finance told us that he was going to take the tariff out of politics and it occurred to me that if his supporters didn't talk tariff in this House they would have not much else to talk about. I know something of the condition of the farmer in Ontario and I take it that in other provinces his condition is about the same. I blame the educational system in Ontario that many of our young men are leaving the rural districts and seeking the cities, in many cases to their great loss. They are told too much about the advantages of professional life, and the advantages of agricultural life are neglected and ignored. Let us spend more money on agricultural colleges and experimental farms and send our boys and girls there to learn scientific farming and modern methods so that they can make farming pay. Sir, it seems strange that there should be such a discrepancy in the reports concerning the Postmaster General's account-the Postmaster General's Report, the Public Accounts and the Auditor General's Report all differ on this matter. I believe, Sir, that in the minister's endeavour to secure a surplus the service in some of its branches is being starved-the letter carriers and the mail carriers are in many instances not half paid. These cases have come under my own observation, and when we are in the estimates I intend to draw the minister's attention to it-I think this is a satire on the Minister of Labour. But, Sir, I wish to say that the farmers of this country are expecting an expression of opinion from the Post-

master General on the question of free mail delivery. This is a question that is growing in favour, and the people, the agriculturists, will soon demand it as a right. I believe, Sir, that the day is near at hand when we shall see the farmer have the daily paper delivered, when the farm house shall have its telephone, and when the electric car will be within easy reach-then home life on the farm will be enjoyable, the boys and the girls will not be discontented and want to go to the city; it will tend to make farm life more attractive, a thing much needed to-day.
This government has been fortunate in many respects but there is one thing left for them to be fortunate in and that is that the people of Canada should turn them out of power before the bad times set in.
